news.title: Trump's 2024 Grocery Photo Op Now Haunts Republicans In The Midterms
news.text:
BEDMINSTER, New Jersey, Aug 15 (Reuters) - Two years after Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump staged a New Jersey press conference flanked by grocery staples to spotlight inflation under Democrats, food prices are still rising despite his pledge to bring them down. The gap between promise and reality now looms as a vulnerability for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Standing between tables piled high with fruit, beef, cereal, milk and other household staples at his Bedminster golf club on August 15, 2024, Trump blamed the Biden administration for sharp increases in groceries. The spectacle, complete with charts showing higher prices, was aimed at undercutting the Democratic nominee, Kamala Harris, and highlighted Trump’s central promise: he alone could tame inflation and lower the cost of living.

Two years on, higher gasoline and grocery prices are squeezing household budgets and turning the cost of living into the top issue for American voters. Voters now give Democrats a slight edge over Republicans in who they view as better stewards of the economy for the first time in nearly a decade, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.

Sheila Carney, a 68-year-old Trump voter, punctuated her frustration with an expletive as she unloaded $70 worth of groceries into her car outside a supermarket not far from Trump’s Bedminster club. The haul was modest: some meat, detergent and a 12-pack of iced tea.

For Carney, the receipt was evidence that the affordability concerns Trump has sometimes dismissed as a Democratic “hoax” remain a daily burden for many Americans.

“This is real. He can say it’s not, but it is,” said Carney, a hospital administration assistant who has delayed retirement while helping pay off her son’s student loans. “He hasn’t brought anything down.”

A Reuters analysis of 26 grocery categories tracked by the Bureau of Labor Statistics and featured in Trump’s Bedminster display found prices have risen 3.4% in the first 19 months of his second term.

That’s less than a quarter of the pace recorded at the same point in former President Joe Biden’s term, but still falls short of Trump’s pledge to lower prices, as surges in coffee, beef and apples have more than offset declines in items including eggs and butter.

A White House official pointed to data on Wednesday that showed U.S. consumer prices barely increased in July from the month before as evidence that inflation is under control.

“The July CPI report is further proof that President Trump’s long-term agenda is delivering: prescription drug and auto insurance costs continue to fall, real wages are rising, and beef prices have cooled while other household essentials like eggs, poultry, and dairy remain low,” the official said.

Lack Of Enthusiasm

A registered Republican, Carney said high grocery and gasoline prices due to the Iran war were among the reasons she had grown disillusioned enough to consider sitting out the midterms, underscoring recent polling suggesting Republicans are less enthusiastic about voting than Democrats.

Carney was one of 17 Republicans and independents Reuters interviewed in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District, a battleground that includes Bedminster and where swing voters and turnout could prove decisive. The race pits Republican incumbent Tom Kean against Democrat Rebecca Bennett, who has sought to capitalize on voters’ frustration over the cost of living.

More than half of those interviewed said they were either undecided or leaning toward Bennett. While grocery prices weighed heavily on many voters, complaints about Kean more often centered on his months-long disappearance from public view earlier this year, which he later attributed to depression.

Their views on the economy mirror those of other Trump supporters Reuters has interviewed in recent months who, despite standing by the president, say financial pressures have dampened their enthusiasm for voting in November. That ambivalence presents another potential challenge for Republicans and raises the stakes for the party’s get-out-the-vote operation.

Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley, recently co-authored research finding that Trump drew stronger support in the 2024 election in counties where inflation outpaced income growth, eroding households’ purchasing power.

With real wages rising only marginally and lagging the pace of broader economic growth, Trebbi said it is likely that pattern will reverse in November.

“I expect the same anti-incumbent shift to happen in 2026, this time possibly weakening Republicans,” he said, describing grocery shopping as a “psychologically salient” reminder of the squeeze on household finances. “Each time one does it, it is the equivalent of a campaign ad against the incumbent.”

Trump Support

To be sure, presidents have limited influence over inflation, which is driven by a range of factors and more directly addressed by the Federal Reserve. And many Republicans appear willing to give Trump the benefit of the doubt, even as his tariffs and the Iran war have contributed to rising prices.

Bonnie Chandler, 64, plans to vote for Kean, saying she believed some companies were keeping prices elevated to make Trump look bad and that the growing influence of the Democratic Party’s progressive faction left her unwilling to consider its candidates.

“I’m going to vote Republican. I’m not a woke person. I’m not a communist. I’m not a socialist,” she said.

Lauren DeGirolamo, a 34-year-old Trump voter, said issues such as education and border security mattered more to her than grocery prices, which she believes have stabilized under Trump following steep increases during the Biden administration.

“I feel grocery prices are pretty much at level with where they were during Biden. I know some of the key things that I look for - eggs - have gone down,” she said, adding that she intended to vote for Republican candidates in November.

According to BLS data, egg prices have fallen nearly 40% under Trump, reflecting a market correction after avian flu-driven shortages triggered a surge that began during Biden’s presidency. Eggs are among six of the 26 categories showing falls since 2025, along with butter, bacon, and cooking fats and oils.

Yet most of the items Trump displayed at Bedminster are now pricier, some by a lot. Uncooked beef has jumped 19.2%, fresh fish and seafood 8.6%, apples 14%, and coffee nearly 23%.

Hitting Close To Home

A Reuters/Ipsos poll that concluded earlier this month found Trump’s net approval rating on his handling of the cost of living was at -47%, down from -6% at the start of his term. It is his weakest issue by a wide margin, trailing his ratings on the economy (-35%) and immigration (-16%).

Bennett told Reuters that if elected she would seek to undo Trump’s tariffs, rein in the Iran war, and restore food stamp benefits to help families struggling to afford groceries.

The issue hits close to home, said Bennett, a military veteran and married mother of two daughters. “This is not an abstract concept to me,” she said. “For example, beef is very expensive, so we don’t buy beef anymore.”

Whether Kean, whose campaign did not respond to requests for comment, can hold on to his seat may depend on voters like Margaret Derkach, who typically votes Republican but is now considering switching her vote if economic conditions don’t improve.

“The cost of living, as far as homes, apartments and food - the necessities - they have gone up. It’s shocking, shocking,” said Derkach, 84, after shopping at discount grocer Aldi.

Though she said Trump “inherited a mess” from Biden, Derkach added, “I am undecided right now. I have to see.”

news.title: Who Is Juan Merchan? Trump Hush Money Judge's Family Under Investigation
news.text: Juan Merchan is the Manhattan judge who became a household name, so to say, for one reason: he ran the courtroom during Donald Trump's hush money trial. These days, though, it's his daughter Loren pulling him back into headlines, after a Democratic fundraising firm she once worked for landed on the radar of federal prosecutors in Chicago. The New York Times first reported the investigation. Merchan oversaw the case that ended in Trump's conviction on 34 felony counts back in May 2024. At the heart of it was a 130,000 dollar payment to Stormy Daniels, the porn star who says she had an affair with Trump and threatened to reveal it during his 2016 campaign. Prosecutors argued Trump falsified business records to keep that payment hidden. Trump wasted no time going after the judge. Just after his arraignment in April 2023, he posted on Truth Social calling Merchan biased and claiming the judge "hates me." He said Merchan "must be changed." Things escalated further in March 2024 once Merchan locked in a trial date and issued a limited gag order. Trump called it illegal, un American, and a violation of his First Amendment rights, framing it as part of a Democratic scheme to weaponize the courts against him. He also suggested, without any evidence, that Merchan was protecting his daughter's political consulting business. Where Loren Merchan Fits InUntil late 2024, Loren Merchan held a vice president role at a firm called Authentic Campaigns Inc, which handles fundraising for Democratic clients. That job is exactly what Trump and his allies have seized on, repeatedly implying she profited somehow from her father's role in the hush money case, again without offering proof. The Chicago InvestigationCourt filings and sources who spoke to the New York Times paint a picture of a federal probe that's been quietly running for close to a year. Back in August last year, the U.S. attorney's office in Chicago sent Authentic Campaigns a subpoena demanding a broad set of internal communications involving its biggest Democratic clients. Investigators wanted to know whether the firm's work crossed any lines, legally speaking. The client roster tied up in this is notable. A grand jury subpoena reviewed by the publication names former Vice President Kamala Harris, former President Joe Biden, New York Governor Kathy Hochul, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, and the Democratic National Committee among the firm's clients. Loren Merchan was named directly in the investigation. Her firm didn't just hand over documents quietly either. Authentic Campaigns fought the subpoena, bringing in former Manhattan U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara as part of its legal team. Eventually, after back and forth negotiations, prosecutors agreed to narrow their ask. What they zeroed in on was surprisingly specific: a 468 dollar payment from Harris' presidential campaign, plus emails between Loren and her father. That detail comes from people close to the investigation who spoke to the publication anonymously, since the probe hasn't wrapped up. Is Anyone Facing Charges?Nobody seems to know for sure. What is clear, according to sources who talked to the publication, is that prosecutors haven't sent out any new subpoenas lately, not to Loren Merchan, not to Authentic Campaigns founder Michael Nellis, not to anyone else tied to the firm. That silence has led some to believe criminal charges aren't imminent, at least not right now. Either way, the case adds to a growing list of examples where federal prosecutors, an institution that used to sit well outside partisan politics, have found themselves caught up in Trump's broader campaign against people he sees as political enemies.
news.summary: Loren Merchan, daughter of the judge who oversaw Trump's hush money trial, has been named in a federal investigation into Democratic fundraising firm Authentic Campaigns.

news.title: Woke 2.0 Will Be Worse
news.text:
Readers familiar with Dr. Seuss’s classic, The Cat in the Hat, will remember the twin chaos agents Thing 1 and Thing 2.

“‘These Things are good Things,’” the Cat reassures the children whose mother has inexplicably left them under the supervision of a fish.

“‘They are tame. Oh, so tame! / They have come here to play.’” 

“I do not like the way that they play!” says the son of the house.

Now here comes Woke 1 and Woke 2.

said U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, quoting an unnamed city councilman in a viral interview for ABC. The congresswoman sheepishly acknowledged that Americans did not like the way Woke 1 played out, while also implicitly announcing that there will soon be, or already is, a Woke 2. And it will be tame. Oh, so tame!

There is, in fact, a new version of wokeness in the making. But just as Thing 2 was fundamentally identical to Thing 1, Woke 2 will not be any different in essence from Woke 1. They are both here to upend the furniture.

Wokeness in all its forms is grievance politics.

Its central idea is that an injustice lies at the heart of America and must be corrected to atone for the historical misery inflicted on groups of innocents.

What is changing in Woke 2 is the account of who those innocents are, and how they have been wronged. Woke 1 was founded on the notion that black women are the most oppressed, and therefore most righteous, of all people. “I’m thinking,” said Kamala Harris in her vice presidential victory speech, “about the generations of women—black women.” She mentioned many other kinds of women, of course, but the list began and ended with “the black women—who are too often overlooked, but so often prove that they are the backbone of this country.”

This approach had rhetorical power, up to a point. It traded on the successes of second-wave feminism and the reality of black slavery in America’s past. But it ran into some problems. Third-wave feminism, as worked out by theorists like Judith Butler, made it basically impossible not to affix the prefix “trans-” wherever the word “woman” appeared. So the flag of Woke 1 became the complicated and confusing progress pride flag—a gay rainbow with black and trans colors intruding from the left.

To make matters worse, the legacy of slavery did not actually touch all the racial minorities that Democrats wanted to bring into their fold. Most Nigerians, for example, had not experienced segregation in the United States. Nor had the millions of unvetted South and Central Americans streaming across the border. They were certainly “people of color.” But so were Chinese, Japanese, and Indian Americans, whose typically enviable life outcomes fit awkwardly into the narrative that the country was built on a ruthless caste system.

The contradictions heightened as Woke 1 faced a series of embarrassments such as Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, the 2023 Supreme Court case in which Asian students complained that admissions officers were discriminating against them in favor of black applicants. Then there were the notorious Trump ’24 ads that pinned Harris to her previous support of taxpayer-funded gender surgeries for federal prison inmates. Placing black women at the center of the moral universe created an unexpected and electorally unworkable set of obligations to illegal immigrants and queer felons.

Clearly, the coalition needed shuffling. And so rearranging the order of priorities in the grievance hierarchy is what the reinvention of woke has actually been about. In place of the black trans woman who defined Woke 1, Woke 2 has chosen as its ideal victim the dispossessed Palestinian liberationist, fighting with Hamas against Israel. This has a number of interesting strategic advantages.

First, the racial argument has been neatly streamlined. Rather than implausibly analogizing every racial group in America to the victims of Jim Crow, Woke 2 presents the black American story as just one instance of a global fight for justice carried out by minorities everywhere and epitomized in the intifada.

In 2023, on a panel for the Democratic Socialists of America, future New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani claimed that “when the boot of the NYPD is on your neck, it’s been laced by the IDF.” He was outlining the blueprint for Woke 2, which takes its cues not from Judith Butler but from post-colonialist Frantz Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth (1961). “Between colonial violence and the insidious violence in which the modern world is steeped,” wrote Fanon, “there is a kind of complicit correlation, a homogeneity.” Therefore, “The colonized, underdeveloped man is today a political creature in the most global sense of the term.”

Recently, in an intriguing interview with The New Yorker’s David Remnick, Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed put forward an argument that connects Fanon’s global struggle to America’s domestic economy. He claimed that pro-Israel politicians are allowing “the money that should be spent taking care of our kids to be sent to a military that has done a genocide.”

In other words, Woke 2’s new order of priorities allows its proponents to suggest that white or white-coded (read: Jewish) oppressors are funneling money away from America’s working poor to fund a worldwide campaign of mass slaughter. Distant as this account is from reality, it is much more ruthlessly focused as a line of woke reasoning. It emphasizes foreign policy and the economy, where the public’s real anger lies, and deftly mutes the discredited claims of LGBTQ extremists.

In practice, any woke administration of any variety will end up imposing pretty much the same bizarre sexual priorities on the country once elected. But for purposes of advertisement, Woke 2 will try to keep its trans members less conspicuous than Woke 1 did, for at least as long as it takes to re-establish national power. Replacing the progress pride flag with the Palestinian flag will distract from the ravages of queer excess while infusing socialist revolution with the moral self-righteousness of anti-white resentment.

Whether this tactic succeeds with voters is another matter.

If it does, though, Americans will discover that both Woke 1 and Woke 2, like Thing 1 and Thing 2, only play nice until they can start pitching over tables. 

If we want to avoid a rerun of the early 2020s, then—to paraphrase Seuss—we will have to get rid of Woke 1 and Woke 2.

news.title: Democrats officially set their 2028 primary calendar, with South Carolina going first
news.text: AUSTIN — Democrats teed up South Carolina to lead a six-state gauntlet of early presidential contests, sealing a 2028 roadmap that pushes Black and Latino voters and labor to the front of the line for choosing the party’s next national leader. After discussions Saturday in Texas, the Democratic National Committee formally anointed South Carolina, with its large African American primary electorate, as the first-in-the-nation state. It will be followed by Nevada, with high numbers of Latinos and powerful labor interests. Next up are New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and then Virginia. As it did in 2024, when then President Joe Biden initially sought re-election, the party committee apparatus put aside its decades-long tradition of kicking off the fight for presidential nominations in Iowa and New Hampshire. The DNC’s early timetable is dispensing entirely with Iowa following its disastrous 2020 caucuses, when issues tallying the votes led to delays and confusion. Party leaders in New Hampshire, traditionally the first-in-the-nation primary state, and Iowa, long the site of first-in-the-nation caucuses, opposed the move. The new calendar would launch the early series of contests in six states from late January through the end of February, after which other states could hold their primaries, too. South Carolina’s primary is to be held on Jan. 22, 2028, Nevada’s on Feb. 1, New Hampshire’s on Feb. 8, New Mexico’s on Feb. 15, Michigan’s on Feb. 22 and Virginia’s on Feb. 29. “Our 2028 nominee, whoever they are, will have to earn the support across the full breadth of America. Every region, every demographic, every generation,” Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said in his opening remarks to committee members on Saturday. “No shortcuts. No coronation. You want to lead this party? Go earn it. Go and earn it.” Martin’s words come as the party is still reckoning with the elevation in 2024 of then-Vice President Kamala Harris, who quickly replaced Biden as the party’s nominee after he stepped aside. Biden, already contending with public doubts over his age and mental fragility, withdrew after he failed to complete sentences and stared off in silence during a televised June debate with Donald Trump. Support from party leaders and donors cratered, as did his position in public polling, forcing Biden to step aside with just 107 days left in the presidential race. He backed Harris and Democratic leaders followed his lead, foregoing any internal contest for the spot. After Harris’ loss, many leaders have lamented the decision not to allow various Democratic contenders to run for the spot. It was Biden as president who first handpicked South Carolina as the party’s leading primary state. The state had salvaged Biden’s candidacy in 2020, when he was on the brink following his own poor showing in Iowa and New Hampshire. news.title: Harris Beating Michelle Obama and AOC Among Young Democrats In 2028 Poll
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris leads former first lady Michelle Obama and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez among young Democrats in a hypothetical 2028 presidential field, according to a new poll. Harris was selected by 28.7 percent of Democratic respondents ages 18 to 34, nearly twice the 14.9 percent who chose Obama. Ocasio-Cortez, the progressive New York Democrat widely known as AOC, placed third with 11.7 percent in the recent Axios-Generation Lab poll, carried out among 1,075 American adults aged 18-34, between July 29 and August 4. None of the three women have announced a 2028 campaign. Young independents favored Obama, who received 11.4 percent, followed by AOC with 9.2 percent and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders with 7.4 percent. Among young Republicans, Vice President JD Vance held a more commanding lead, receiving 31.5 percent. Donald Trump Jr. followed with 10.7 percent, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio received 9.7 percent. The findings came amid broad dissatisfaction among younger Americans: 66 percent disapproved of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 96 percent expressed concern about the cost of rent, groceries, gas or utilities. Generation Lab CEO Cyrus Beschloss characterized the broader mood as “thumbs-down on everything,” saying young people were dissatisfied with the president, the economy and both political parties. Of those surveyed, 37 percent identified as Democrats, 26 percent as Republicans and 29 percent as independents. The poll had an overall margin of error of +/- 3.01 percentage points. What the Poll Shows About Harris, Obama and AOC Harris’ 28.7 percent support was greater than the combined backing for Obama and Ocasio-Cortez, who received 26.6 percent between them. However, the former vice president did not command a majority, underscoring how unsettled the prospective Democratic field remains at this early stage. Of the three, Harris is the only one to have run for president or held elected office nationwide. She replaced former President Joe Biden at the top of the Democratic ticket in 2024 before losing the election to Trump. Harris later ruled out a campaign for California governor in 2026, a decision that left open the possibility of another White House bid. Obama’s second-place showing is notable because she has never held elected office and has repeatedly rejected suggestions that she could run for president. During a 2018 appearance with students in New York, Obama said that politics had never been her chosen path and that she did not want to be president. The former first lady also performed better among independents than she did among Democrats relative to the other prospective candidates. Obama led the independent field with 11.4 percent, while AOC placed second with 9.2 percent. The result indicates that Obama’s appeal in the survey extended beyond Democratic identifiers, although her support remained in the low double digits. AOC, meanwhile, has built a national profile as one of the Democratic Party’s most prominent progressives since first winning election to Congress in 2018. Her policy agenda has included proposals addressing climate change, housing costs and economic inequality; in August, she and Sanders reintroduced legislation intended to renovate public housing and create union jobs. Despite her prominence among younger progressives, AOC trailed Harris by 17 percentage points among young Democrats and finished 3.2 points behind Obama. Trump and Republicans Struggle With Young Americans The poll also found widespread opposition to Trump among young Americans. Sixty-six percent disapproved of his job performance, including 54 percent who strongly disapproved, while 34 percent approved. Republicans also trailed Democrats when respondents were asked which party they trusted more to reduce the cost of living. Some 32 percent percent chose Republicans, compared with 26 percent who selected Democrats. The largest group, 36 percent, trusted neither party—giving “neither” a 14-point advantage over the GOP. That result is particularly significant given the scale of respondents’ economic concerns. Although nearly all of those surveyed expressed some concern about the cost of essentials, fewer than one-quarter trusted the president’s party to bring those expenses down. The findings point to dissatisfaction with both major parties rather than a decisive shift toward Democrats. Polls have been known to underestimate Trump's popularity, with the president outperforming pre-election expectations in three presidential campaigns. Newsweek contacted the White House via email on Saturday for comment. In June, when the White House responded to Trump's approval rating hitting an all-time low with Big Data Poll, which has previously showed some of Trump's highest approval ratings, spokesperson Davis Ingle told Newsweek the 2024 election was "the ultimate poll." "No other President in history has accomplished more for the American people than President Trump, who is working tirelessly to create jobs, cool inflation, increase housing affordability, and more," Ingle said.
news.summary: A youth poll puts Harris ahead of Obama and AOC, as young Americans voice discontent with Trump and both major parties.

news.title: This Might Be the Most Brutal Diagnosis of AOC You'll Ever Hear
news.text:
Kellyanne Conway appeared on Fox News’s The Five this week and gave a blunt yet extremely fair assessment of Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.): she's not actually doing her job.

"AOC stands for Always On Camera," Conway said. "She is a performer, not a reformer. She went to Washington to legislate; that's her job. She's a pontificator, not a legislator."

Conway piled on by pointing out that, in four years under President Joe Biden, AOC passed one bill. One. Conway's point was simple: if you're not good at legislating, you find something else to be good at, like living online, playing with your hair, and giggling every time someone asks whether you'd be fit to serve as commander-in-chief. Conway didn't think that was funny. With the whole world watching, she said, that kind of response would be "embarrassing and a disaster."

Just watch The Brink of War and imagine AOC in a similar situation. You can’t, because she’s an absolute joke. But I digress.

AOC has tried to distance herself from her old positions by claiming her rhetoric from years ago doesn't reflect where she is today. Conway found that laughable. Five years isn't ancient history, and she made the point with a sharp comparison: does AOC's position change with the seasons, too? If it's raining, does she flip? If it's October instead of April? Conway called the whole excuse disgraceful, and said both failed Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong and AOC had proven themselves untrustworthy to voters.

 ICYMI: What? Stephen A. Smith Hints He Could Become a Republican.

Conway also gave AOC credit for one thing. She started as a bartender who knocked off longtime incumbent Joe Crowley in a primary nobody saw coming. That, Conway said, was the best thing AOC ever did. Everything since has traded on being the fresh face, the disruptor. But by 2028, AOC will have spent ten years in Washington voting the party line, while also proving herself to be extremely radical. For example, she was also one of only ten Democrats to vote against a resolution condemning the October 7, 2023 attack, just eleven days after it happened.

And Conway wasn't finished with the receipts.

She explained how 2024 was a disaster for AOC's political brand. Kamala Harris spent over a billion dollars and lost anyway. AOC endorsed Jamaal Bowman in his primary, and he lost. She endorsed Cori Bush, and she lost, too.

“AOC stands for Always On Camera!" @KellyannePolls calls AOC a “performer, not a reformer,” arguing the congresswoman is more focused on viral moments than delivering results for voters. pic.twitter.com/3KaYx0nkm1— The Five (@TheFive) August 15, 2026

Make no mistake about it, Conway's larger argument wasn't really about policy. It was about authenticity, or the lack of it. She called AOC a "performative progressive," someone running “stunts and grunts” to sway voters, rather than legislating on their behalf. Conway doesn't think Americans are buying it anymore. Voters who tweet first and think third and fourth, she said, will pay a price for it.

She's right. AOC has spent a decade cultivating an image as the insurgent outsider fighting the establishment. Conway just pointed out what should have been obvious all along: the insurgent outsider has become the establishment, and yet she has nothing to show for it.

news.title: 10 Key Congressional Races That Could Decide Control of Washington
news.text:
For the first two years of President Donald Trump’s second term, Republicans have commanded a Washington trifecta, holding the White House, the Senate, and the House of Representatives.

That dominance is now under pressure, with the midterm elections fast approaching and the GOP facing a difficult fight to preserve its grip on power.

A July Daily Mail/JL Partners poll found voters favoring a Democratic candidate in the November midterms by more than nine points, widening by a full point from the previous month.

Trump has also openly questioned the party’s prospects, voicing concern over whether conservative voters will turn out this fall when his own name is not on the ballot.

‘If I don’t run, will those people go out and vote, and that’s the one thing I can’t tell,’ Trump said recently. 

Even so, Republicans are outpacing Democrats in fundraising, both at the national level and in critical battleground contests. That financial edge underscores a central reality of the midterms: control of Congress will likely come down not to party strategists in Washington, but to turnout in the competitive districts and states that will decide the map.

Below are the races most likely to shape the next Congress, as scandals, explosive allegations, and family turmoil upend some of the most closely watched contests in the country.

The US Senate

Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the Senate, and Democrats need to pick up at least four of them to control the upper chamber in the next Congress. The following 10 Senate races are likely to determine control of the Senate.

North Carolina Senate: Roy Cooper (D) versus Michael Whatley (R)

Cooper, North Carolina’s former governor, is facing off against Republican Michael Whatley, former chairman of the Republican National Committee. Cooper has won statewide elections for both Governor and Attorney General, while Whatley has not run for statewide office. Whatley enjoys a close relationship with Trump, as well as GOP donors due to his past role at the RNC, and he is helped by the fact that Trump has won North Carolina three times. Still, Democrats, including Cooper and current Governor Josh Stein, show that they can also win statewide by avoiding nationalizing races and focusing on local issues. Republican incumbent Thom Tillis chose not to seek re-election and has become a thorn in Trump’s side in his last few months in Washington, clashing with some of the most high-profile members of his administration, including former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem over disaster relief funds and assistance. The seat is rated as ‘lean Democrat‘ by the Cook Political Report.

Maine Senate: Susan Collins (R) versus Troy Jackson (D)

Fiercely independent GOP Senator Susan is in the midst of a tough re-election battle in Maine, which has one of the oldest electorates in the country. After her previous opponent Graham Platner dropped out of the race amid a slew of allegations of sexual misconduct and abuse, which he denies, Maine Democrats selected former state Senate President Troy Jackson as their nominee. But he has always been marred by his own controversies, including a revelation that he fathered children with his second cousin. The seat is rated to be a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

Georgia Senate: Jon Ossoff (D) versus Mike Collins (R)

Incumbent Democrat golden boy Jon Ossoff is seen as one of the party’s rising stars at the age of 39. Still, he faces one of the toughest reelection maps in the country in Georgia, a state Trump won in 2024 despite his clashes with fellow Republican and the state’s outgoing governor Brian Kemp. Ossoff’s prospects became slightly more favorable after House GOP lawmaker Mike Collins emerged victorious in the Republican Primary despite a slew of personal and personnel issues. It has been previously uncovered by Our News Outlet that Collins’ son-in-law shared white supremacist rhetoric, and that his top advisors have been referred to the House Ethics Committee over an alleged misuse of funds. Despite the controversies, Collins is likely to be helped in the race by spending to drive GOP voters to the polls in support of the gubernatorial nominee, Rick Jackson, who is independently wealthy. The seat is rated as ‘lean Democrat‘ by the Cook Political Report.

New Hampshire Senate: Chris Pappas (D) versus John Sununu (R)

Outgoing incumbent Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen declined to seek re-election to a fourth term in New Hampshire, in a seat which Democrats are likely to still hold in November. But Republcians will not go down without a fight. The state’s GOP governor, Kelly Ayotte, is highly popular, and the Sununu name is one of the most recognized in New Hampshire politics. John H Sununu, the father of the two Sununu brothers, Chris and John, served as the 75th Governor of New Hampshire in the 1980’s and was also White House Chief of Staff under President George HW Bush. Chris Sununu, John’s brother, served as Governor of New Hampshire, holding office from January 2017 to January 2025. John has also been elected to both the US House and US Senate by Granite Staters, most recently serving in the Senate from 2003 to 2009. He has since been in the private sector. Sununu still has to formally become the nominee, as New Hampshire’s primary does not take place until September. The seat is rated ‘lean Democrat‘ by the Cook Political Report.

Ohio Senate: Jon Husted (R) versus Sherrod Brown (D)

Incumbent Jon Husted is running statewide for a full term after being appointed to Ohio’s US Senate seat after JD Vance vacated the post for the vice presidency. Sherrod Brown, a 73-year-old Democrat, is mounting a comeback bid for his old Senate seat. He formerly served in Washington for three decades. The Daily Mail has reported that Brown’s claims that he’s fighting for Ohio farmers appear to be at odds with his support of Joe Biden’s American Rescue Act, and video unearthed by Our News Outlet showed him complaining about ‘black and brown’ people at the US Capitol. The seat is rated to be a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

Iowa Senate: Ashley Hinson (R) versus Josh Turek (D)

In Iowa, Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson is on the statewide ballot for the first time, having represented a seat on the eastern side of the state since 2021, after flipping it in 2020. Josh Turek, a state lawmaker, made it out of a bruising primary after getting boosts from major Democrats. One of his biggest backers has been former President Barack Obama, who filmed a basketball-themed ad with Turek, a former Paralympic hooper. Incumbent Senator Joni Ernst chose not to seek re-election for another term in the Hawkeye state. Iowa leans Republican, but Hinson could be negatively impacted by Democrat Rob Sand performing well in the gubernatorial race. The seat is rated ‘lean Republican’ by the Cook Political Report.

Michigan Senate: Mike Rogers (R) versus Abdul El-Sayed (D)

Michigan is one of the true toss-ups in November, as Progressive insurgent Abdul El-Sayed was declared the winner of a rollercoaster Democratic primary for the US Senate after squeaking by with a slim victory over Congresswoman Haley Stevens. His single-point win raises new questions about whether his strength among base voters can translate to a general election this fall, as Democrats look to flip four seats necessary to secure a majority in the upper chamber. El-Sayed fared well with Arab-American and younger voters, while Stevens nabbed support from older Democrats as well as African-American voters who do not seem ready to back El-Sayed in November. Rogers, a former House GOP lawmaker, has been biding his time as the GOP’s presumptive nominee for months, waiting on a challenger to emerge from the Democratic Party. The seat is rated to as a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

Texas Senate: Ken Paxton (R) versus James Talarico (D)

Republicans hope to pull out a win by the skin of their teeth in Texas, where the State’s Attorney General Ken Paxton won a bruising GOP primary to face off against James Talarico, a state legislator. Paxton won his primary with Trump’s endorsement, ousting incumbent Senator John Cornyn, and Talarico beat out House Democratic firebrand Jasmine Crockett in his primary. Paxton has to overcome allegations of adultery amid a messy divorce, and a past impeachment from his post before being acquitted by fellow Republicans in the Texas Senate, all ahead of the general election. But he was able to make it out of the primary full of Christian evangelical voters, even with metric tons of personal baggage. Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott is running for a historic fourth consecutive four-year term in the Lone Star State, something that will definitely help drive turnout for Paxton statewide. The seat is rated as ‘lean Republican’ by the Cook Political Report.

Nebraska Senate: Pete Ricketts (R) versus Dan Osborn (I)

Independent Dan Osborn is back on the ballot in the Cornhusker state two years after losing to a Republican statewide in 2024. This time, he’s facing Pete Ricketts, the state’s incumbent GOP Senator and former Governor. Osborn’s campaigning has been marred by several eyebrow-raising moments, including revelations that he has paid himself and family members nearly half a million dollars in campaign funds, and that his daughter participates in NSFW platforms. Ricketts is likely to hold the seat in November, and the seat is rated ‘likely Republican by the Cook Political Report.

Alaska Senate: Dan Sullivan (R) versus Mary Peltola (D)

In the Last Frontier state, incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan, who has served as Alaska’s junior Senator since 2015 is facing off against Mary Peltola, a former House lawmaker. During her years in Washington, Peltola was known for her moderate voting record, something Sullivan will most likely have to contend with this year. Alaska has not yet held its primary election, and Dan S Sullivan is in a contest with 15 candidates, including Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher. Alaska’s use of ranked-choice voting also complicates its elections. The seat is rated to as a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

The House of Representatives

Republicans currently have a majority in the US House of Representatives, 218 to 212. The lower chamber currently has four vacancies, three Democrat and one Republican. To gain a majority, Democrats need to flip at least three seats. 

These are the tightest races in the lead-up to November involving missing congressmen, shocking abuse claims, and more.

New Jersey’s 7th District: Rep. Tom Kean Jr (R) versus Rebecca Bennett (D)

Incumbent Republican Congressman Tom Kean Jr of New Jersey missed over 140 consecutive votes earlier this year in an absence he attributed to depression upon his return to Washington. During the hiatus, he was overly cryptic, questioned by both local and national media about his secrecy, and raised doubts about his ability to serve his constituents. In November, Kean faces Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot who easily bested a trio of other Democrats for the nomination. The seat is rated as a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

Ohio’s 7th District: Rep. Max Miller (R) versus Brian Poindexter (D)

The drama is overflowing in Ohio’s 7th District as domestic ‘abuse’ allegations plague the run of Trump-backed Max Miller, who currently holds the seat. His ex-wife Emily Moreno, the daughter of sitting Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, has made scathing claims against him involving their two-year-old daughter, which he has denied. However, his standing with voters has taken a steep dive since the physical abuse allegations, first reported by Our News Outlet, came to light. The Cook Political Report rates this seat as a ‘toss up.’

Pennsylvania’s 10th District: Rep. Scott Perry (R) versus Janelle Stelson (D) 

Incumbent Republican Scott Perry is set for a rematch with Janelle Stelson. He beat her by the skin of his teeth in 2024, with 50.5 percent of the vote to his opponent’s 49.3 percent. Despite being in a district that President Donald Trump won by five points, Perry is a member of the ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus, raising questions about how good of a match he is for the district. The seat is rated to be a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

Virginia’s 2nd District: Rep. Jen Kiggans (R) versus Former Representative Elaine Luria (D)

Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans is set for another face-off with Democrat Elaine Luria, whom she wrestled Virginia’s Second District from in 2022. Luria represented the seat for two terms after winning it in a midterm election in 2018 during the last time Trump was in the White House, ousting Republican Scott Taylor. Both Kiggans and Luria are veterans, having served in the US Navy, and they seek to represent a seat that is home to nearly 90,000 veterans. The seat is rated as a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

New York’s 17th District: Mike Lawler (R) versus Cait Conley (D)

A big race to keep an eye on is incumbent Republican Mike Lawler versus veteran Cait Conley in New York. Lawler is under scrutiny for his close friendship with Max Miller, who is facing abuse allegations, and lavish spending on the campaign trail. He also recently admitted that he was ‘arrested for DWI’ in his younger days. The seat is rated ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report. 

Ohio’s 9th District: Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D) versus Derek Merrin (R) 

Incumbent Democrat Marcy Kaptur is running for her 23rd term in the House this November, facing Republican Derek Merrin. The race is another rematch, and Merrin, a former state lawmaker, lost to Kaptur by 2,383 votes in 2024. Kaptur’s bid is complicated by her recent involvement in a car accident, after which she is undergoing physical rehabilitation. The seat is rated a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

Michigan’s 7th District: Rep. Tom Barrett (R) versus William Lawrence (D)

Freshman Republican Tom Barrett has an uphill battle in his first-ever re-election bid this November. He is facing off against William Lawrence, a progressive climate organizer with a 13-year-old felony case related to his activism. During a 2013 protest at an Enbridge Energy pipeline work site, Lawrence chained himself to construction equipment and refused to leave. He was charged with resisting and obstructing police, which is a felony, and the conviction was later expunged. The seat is rated to be a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

Iowa’s 1st District: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) versus Christina Bohannan (D)

Incumbent Republican Mariannette Miller-Meeks is no stranger to tough elections. After winning her first federal race in 2020 by 6 votes, Miller-Meeks, like Kiggans, has had a tough job of keeping both her base happy but still working to satisfy independent voters. This time around, she is facing Christina Bohannan, a lawyer, engineer, and former State Representative. Miller-Meeks, like Hinson, could be hurt by a strong turnout for Democrat Rob Sand in the race for governor if his supporters vote the whole ballot. The seat is rated as a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

Texas’ 34th District: Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D) versus Eric Flores (R)

Incumbent Democrat Vicente Gonzalez is facing Republican Eric Flores in a redrawn seat this November. The district has trended towards the GOP in recent years, and Flores believes that voters don’t understand Democratic opposition to Trump’s immigration policies in a heavily Hispanic region. Gonzalez, meanwhile, has characterized Trump’s approach as ‘America Last.’ The seat is rated to be a ‘toss up’ by the Cook Political Report.

Nebraska’s 2nd District: Denise Powell (D) versus Brinker Harding (R) 

Republican Congressman and retired US Air Force Brigadier General Don Bacon chose not to seek re-election in 2026, after winning his 2024 race for the GOP despite Kamala Harris winning his district by five points and its electoral vote. That leaves one of the most vulnerable GOP House seats in the country open with no incumbent. Republican Brinker Harding, an Omaha City Councilman, faces off against Denise Powell, a mom and small business owner in November for Bacon’s seat. The seat is rated as ‘lean Democrat‘ by the Cook Political Report.

California’s 22nd District: Rep. David Valadao (R) versus Randy Villegas (D) 

Incumbent Republican David Valadao has maintained an independent streak throughout his six terms in the US House of Representatives. If reelected, he would be the only GOP member of the House still standing in the second half of Trump’s second term, despite having voted to impeach him in 2021. In November, Valadao faces Randy Villegas, an educator and activist. The seat is rated a Toss-Up by the Cook Political Report.

Michigan Senate: Mike Rogers (R) versus Abdul El-Sayed (D)

Mike Rogers (R) and Abdul El-Sayed (D)

Abdul El-Sayed oversaw animal 'slaughterhouse' as over 4,000 pets killed under his watch

Michigan is one of the true toss-ups in November, as Progressive insurgent Abdul El-Sayed was declared the winner of a rollercoaster Democratic primary for the US Senate after squeaking by with a slim victory over Congresswoman Haley Stevens. His single-point win raises new questions about whether his strength among base voters can translate to a general election this fall, as Democrats look to flip four seats necessary to secure a majority in the upper chamber. El-Sayed fared well with Arab-American and younger voters, while Stevens nabbed support from older Democrats as well as African-American voters who do not seem ready to back El-Sayed in November. Rogers, a former House GOP lawmaker, has been biding his time as the GOP's presumptive nominee for months, waiting on a challenger to emerge from the Democratic Party. The seat is rated to as a 'toss up' by the Cook Political Report.

Texas Senate: Ken Paxton (R) versus James Talarico (D)

Ken Paxton (R) and James Talarico (D)

Republicans hope to pull out a win by the skin of their teeth in Texas, where the State's Attorney General Ken Paxton won a bruising GOP primary to face off against James Talarico, a state legislator. Paxton won his primary with Trump's endorsement, ousting incumbent Senator John Cornyn, and Talarico beat out House Democratic firebrand Jasmine Crockett in his primary. Paxton has to overcome allegations of adultery amid a messy divorce, and a past impeachment from his post before being acquitted by fellow Republicans in the Texas Senate, all ahead of the general election. But he was able to make it out of the primary full of Christian evangelical voters, even with metric tons of personal baggage. Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott is running for a historic fourth consecutive four-year term in the Lone Star State, something that will definitely help drive turnout for Paxton statewide. The seat is rated as 'lean Republican' by the Cook Political Report.

Nebraska Senate: Pete Ricketts (R) versus Dan Osborn (I)

Pete Ricketts (R) and Dan Osborn (I)

Astronomical sum Democrats' secret Senate weapon paid to wife and 'exotic dancer' daughter

Independent Dan Osborn is back on the ballot in the Cornhusker state two years after losing to a Republican statewide in 2024. This time, he's facing Pete Ricketts, the state's incumbent GOP Senator and former Governor. Osborn's campaigning has been marred by several eyebrow-raising moments, including revelations that he has paid himself and family members nearly half a million dollars in campaign funds, and that his daughter participates in NSFW platforms. Ricketts is likely to hold the seat in November, and the seat is rated 'likely Republican by the Cook Political Report.

Alaska Senate: Dan Sullivan (R) versus Mary Peltola (D)

Dan S Sullivan (R) and Mary Peltola (D)

In the Last Frontier state, incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan, who has served as Alaska's junior Senator since 2015 is facing off against Mary Peltola, a former House lawmaker. During her years in Washington, Peltola was known for her moderate voting record, something Sullivan will most likely have to contend with this year. Alaska has not yet held its primary election, and Dan S Sullivan is in a contest with 15 candidates, including Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher. Alaska's use of ranked-choice voting also complicates its elections. The seat is rated to as a 'toss up' by the Cook Political Report.

The House of Representatives

Republicans currently have a majority in the US House of Representatives, 218 to 212. The lower chamber currently has four vacancies, three Democrat and one Republican. To gain a majority, Democrats need to flip at least three seats. 

These are the tightest races in the lead-up to November involving missing congressmen, shocking abuse claims, and more.

New Jersey’s 7th District: Rep. Tom Kean Jr (R) versus Rebecca Bennett (D)

Rep. Tom Kean Jr (R) and Rebecca Bennett (D) 

Incumbent Republican Congressman Tom Kean Jr of New Jersey missed over 140 consecutive votes earlier this year in an absence he attributed to depression upon his return to Washington. During the hiatus, he was overly cryptic, questioned by both local and national media about his secrecy, and raised doubts about his ability to serve his constituents. In November, Kean faces Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot who easily bested a trio of other Democrats for the nomination. The seat is rated as a 'toss up' by the Cook Political Report.

Ohio's 7th District: Rep. Max Miller (R) versus Brian Poindexter (D)

Rep. Max Miller (R) and Brian Poindexter (D)

Photos expose Trump-backed congressman's 'abuse': Senator's daughter reveals scalding water attack

The drama is overflowing in Ohio's 7th District as domestic 'abuse' allegations plague the run of Trump-backed Max Miller, who currently holds the seat. His ex-wife Emily Moreno, the daughter of sitting Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, has made scathing claims against him involving their two-year-old daughter, which he has denied. However, his standing with voters has taken a steep dive since the physical abuse allegations, first reported by the Daily Mail, came to light. The Cook Political Report rates this seat as a 'toss up.'

Pennsylvania’s 10th District: Rep. Scott Perry (R) versus Janelle Stelson (D) 

Rep. Scott Perry (R) and Janelle Stelson (D)

Incumbent Republican Scott Perry is set for a rematch with Janelle Stelson. He beat her by the skin of his teeth in 2024, with 50.5 percent of the vote to his opponent's 49.3 percent. Despite being in a district that President Donald Trump won by five points, Perry is a member of the ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus, raising questions about how good of a match he is for the district. The seat is rated to be a 'toss up' by the Cook Political Report.

Virginia’s 2nd District: Rep. Jen Kiggans (R) versus Former Representative Elaine Luria (D)

Rep. Jen Kiggans (R) versus Former Representative Elaine Luria (D)

Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans is set for another face-off with Democrat Elaine Luria, whom she wrestled Virginia's Second District from in 2022. Luria represented the seat for two terms after winning it in a midterm election in 2018 during the last time Trump was in the White House, ousting Republican Scott Taylor. Both Kiggans and Luria are veterans, having served in the US Navy, and they seek to represent a seat that is home to nearly 90,000 veterans. The seat is rated as a 'toss up' by the Cook Political Report.

New York's 17th District: Mike Lawler (R) versus Cait Conley (D)

Mike Lawler (R) and Cait Conley (D)

A big race to keep an eye on is incumbent Republican Mike Lawler versus veteran Cait Conley in New York. Lawler is under scrutiny for his close friendship with Max Miller, who is facing abuse allegations, and lavish spending on the campaign trail. He also recently admitted that he was 'arrested for DWI' in his younger days. The seat is rated 'toss up' by the Cook Political Report. 

Ohio’s 9th District: Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D) versus Derek Merrin (R) 

Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D) and Derek Merrin (R)

Incumbent Democrat Marcy Kaptur is running for her 23rd term in the House this November, facing Republican Derek Merrin. The race is another rematch, and Merrin, a former state lawmaker, lost to Kaptur by 2,383 votes in 2024. Kaptur's bid is complicated by her recent involvement in a car accident, after which she is undergoing physical rehabilitation. The seat is rated a 'toss up' by the Cook Political Report.

Michigan’s 7th District: Rep. Tom Barrett (R) versus William Lawrence (D)

Rep. Tom Barrett (R) and William Lawrence (D)

Freshman Republican Tom Barrett has an uphill battle in his first-ever re-election bid this November. He is facing off against William Lawrence, a progressive climate organizer with a 13-year-old felony case related to his activism. During a 2013 protest at an Enbridge Energy pipeline work site, Lawrence chained himself to construction equipment and refused to leave. He was charged with resisting and obstructing police, which is a felony, and the conviction was later expunged. The seat is rated to be a 'toss up' by the Cook Political Report.

Iowa’s 1st District: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) versus Christina Bohannan (D)

Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) and Christina Bohannan (D)

Incumbent Republican Mariannette Miller-Meeks is no stranger to tough elections. After winning her first federal race in 2020 by 6 votes, Miller-Meeks, like Kiggans, has had a tough job of keeping both her base happy but still working to satisfy independent voters. This time around, she is facing Christina Bohannan, a lawyer, engineer, and former State Representative. Miller-Meeks, like Hinson, could be hurt by a strong turnout for Democrat Rob Sand in the race for governor if his supporters vote the whole ballot. The seat is rated as a 'toss up' by the Cook Political Report.

Texas’ 34th District: Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D) versus Eric Flores (R)

Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D) and Eric Flores (R)

Incumbent Democrat Vicente Gonzalez is facing Republican Eric Flores in a redrawn seat this November. The district has trended towards the GOP in recent years, and Flores believes that voters don't understand Democratic opposition to Trump's immigration policies in a heavily Hispanic region. Gonzalez, meanwhile, has characterized Trump's approach as 'America Last.' The seat is rated to be a 'toss up' by the Cook Political Report.

Nebraska’s 2nd District: Denise Powell (D) versus Brinker Harding (R) 

Denise Powell (D) and Brinker Harding (R)

Republican Congressman and retired US Air Force Brigadier General Don Bacon chose not to seek re-election in 2026, after winning his 2024 race for the GOP despite Kamala Harris winning his district by five points and its electoral vote. Republican Brinker Harding, an Omaha City Councilman, faces off against Denise Powell, a mom and small business owner in November for Bacon's seat. news.title: Jon Ossoff clearly has his eyes on something beyond his Senate seat
news.text:
His political biography has the structure of a story Democrats badly need right now. In April 2017, at 29 years old, with no elective experience and a resume built on documentary filmmaking and a congressional staff job, he ran in a special election for Georgia’s 6th District. The seat had belonged to Republicans since Newt Gingrich won it in 1978. Tom Price had just vacated it to become Trump’s Secretary of Health and Human Services. Democrats, smelling blood in the Atlanta suburbs, poured money in. Ossoff raised $8.3 million before the first vote was cast. He finished first in a crowded field with 48.1% of the vote, nearly 30 points ahead of Republican Karen Handel, but fell just short of the 50% threshold Georgia requires to avoid a runoff. Two months later, Handel beat him, 51.8% to 48.2%.

It was, at the time, treated as a referendum Democrats lost. The most expensive House race in American history at the time, and they had nothing to show for it.

Three years later, Ossoff was back, this time challenging incumbent Republican Sen. David Perdue for a Senate seat. In November 2020, Perdue finished ahead of him with 49.7% of the vote to Ossoff’s 47.9%, again just shy of the majority Georgia law requires. Again, a runoff.

What happened between November 2020 and Jan. 5, 2021, is a matter of public record that the Ossoff campaign did not manufacture, but benefited from completely.

President Donald Trump spent the two months between the general election and the Georgia runoffs insisting the presidential election had been stolen from him. Perdue, to maintain good standing with Trump, had to buy into the narrative, and it cost him. It drove down Republican turnout in a state where the party’s voters were being told simultaneously that their votes would not count, but at the same time, the runoff election was the last line of defense. No one in Trump’s orbit could prove the fraud he hollered about. Georgia’s Republican secretary of state certified the results and said there was no evidence of fraud. None of it moved Trump. By the time Jan. 6 arrived and the Capitol was breached, Georgia had already voted. Ossoff beat Perdue by nearly 45,000 votes. The Senate split 50-50, and Vice President Kamala Harris would hold the tiebreaker in just two more weeks.

The loss of GOP Senate control set up the scenario for Joe Biden and the Democratic Party to pass the $2 trillion American Rescue Plan, which helped contribute to the inflationary spiral that lasted into late 2022.

Ossoff is now 37, in his first Senate term, and running for reelection in a Georgia that Republicans are convinced they can still win. He is also, whether he will say so or not, a figure Democrats are projecting something much larger onto. On Polymarket, the prediction market that has become a go-to gauge for pundits and the press, Ossoff sits at 14%, second only to Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA) at 19% in the 2028 Democratic presidential field, and ahead of Harris, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), and every other name in the party.

For a first-term senator who has not won a general election since January 2021, it is a remarkable position to occupy. When asked directly, he gives the standard answer. He told CNN recently he has “no interest in running for president in 2028.” A senator genuinely uninterested in a presidential run does not publicly brand Trump’s advisers “the Mar-a-Lago mafia” or grill Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on the cost of the Iran war in exchanges clearly engineered for circulation. The “Epstein class” line. The “world’s most famous sore loser” characterization ahead of Trump’s primetime election-fraud address. Denying any interest in running for president before winning his Senate race is standard pablum, and certainly not his actual intentions.

What the clips and focused media attention do reveal is how carefully Ossoff has staked out the progressive positions along with the performance, while walking a tightrope that has become difficult for Democrats to walk in the current political environment. He does not use the language of the Bernie Sanders and AOC wing of the party. He does not call for Medicare for All or abolishing ICE. But he has pushed aggressively for Medicaid expansion, Affordable Care Act tax credit extensions, and a public option (which is essentially Medicare for All without the title). On immigration, he has run a formal Senate investigation into alleged reports of abuse in ICE detention facilities, called agents “roving gangs of masked men,” and fought the Trump administration’s plan to convert a Georgia warehouse into a detention center holding up to 10,000 immigrants. He’s ditched the slogans while still anchoring himself to those positions, but doing so in a way that he could still win Georgia in November.

What makes Ossoff’s positioning unusual, and what separates him structurally from other Democrats the base has chewed through in recent years, is that he is not paying the normal price (yet) for being what he is. His profile on immigration is enforcement paired with legal protections, a lane that requires him to hold two things at once without lurching toward either extreme. In any other Democratic cycle, the balancing act alone would be enough to draw fire. Whether that is the desire for Democrats to take control of Congress or a strategic lane remains to be seen.

The one place where Ossoff broke from the party’s mainstream, on some Israel military funding votes, buys him credibility that other Democrats casting the same votes would not enjoy. He is Jewish, and the votes carry a weight that a non-Jewish senator casting the same ballots would not enjoy. A statement his office released last July captures the balance he is trying to hold. He voted to block a sale of rifles to Israel, citing “the extreme mass deprivation of civilians in Gaza, including the intolerable starvation of children” under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, and noted the weapons would likely have gone to police forces controlled by Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. On the same night, he voted against blocking a separate sale of air-to-ground munitions, writing that Israel’s capacity to defend itself against rocket and missile attack depends on its air force. Hamas, he wrote, “a despicable terrorist organization, started this horrific round of conflict with the brutal massacre of October 7th, 2023.”

Whether that is a sincere expression of a position shaped by faith and identity or a calculated insurance policy against the attack line that comes from the Democratic Party’s progressive wing, including the Democratic Socialists of America faction that is openly hostile to Israel and gaining traction within the party, is the kind of question the Ossoff story refuses to answer cleanly, but it gives him some cover in the short term.

Compare him to Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-PA), another Jewish Democrat with national ambitions. Shapiro’s job approval sits near 60%. His crossover appeal with Republicans and independents is genuine and documented. Meanwhile, the far-left has spent two years calling him “Genocide Josh” for positions on Israel that are not all that materially different from Ossoff’s. The difference is not policy. Ossoff gives the base the performance they are looking for. He makes the fight visible. Shapiro, in an executive role, has to govern. The base does not want governance right now. It wants someone who will “fight,” and Ossoff is staking out that ground.

The DSA types who will come after him in a primary are a real problem, just not necessarily the most immediate one. His more pressing task is winning reelection in a state that his party has carried twice in four years, both times narrowly and under circumstances that may not recur. If he loses Georgia in November, the 2028 speculation collapses with it. There is no presidential primary lane for a one-term senator who lost his reelection bid. The entire architecture of the next chapter of his political life rests on holding a seat in a state Trump won, but by a little more than two points.

Rahm Emanuel, who has recently and accurately diagnosed the Democratic base’s hostility to its own winning Democrats with characteristic precision, is not particularly popular with the activist wing that has warmed to Ossoff. Emanuel argues the base rejects winning Democrats who don’t perform the fight. Ossoff is the counterargument, at least for now. The base will accept someone who performs the fight and hits the right symbolic notes, which means the disagreement was never really about ideology but rather about the kind of performative politics that has become part of the mainstream in today’s culture.

Whether Ossoff can hold that position, win Georgia, and keep the 2028 door open while the base’s patience for anything short of the full progressive program continues to thin is the question his career is currently structured around and remains to be seen. The predictive markets, the viral clips, and the new look and demeanor are winning people over for the moment.

Jay Caruso (@JayCaruso) is a writer living in Florida.

The boyish face that made him a cable news fixture during the 2017 Georgia special election, the one that Republicans in the 6th Congressional District hung in mailers next to the word “outsider,” has been replaced by […]

news.title: Trump’s 2024 photo op comes back to haunt Republicans in the midterms
news.text:
Two years after Donald Trump staged a press conference in New Jersey where he stood alongside basic household groceries to attack Democratic inflation, food costs continue to climb.

At his Bedminster golf club on August 15, 2024, he stood amidst displays stacked with meat, fruit, cereal, milk and standard pantry items while laying the blame for steep grocery price hikes on the Biden administration. The event, featuring charts illustrating rising costs, targeted Democratic nominee Kamala Harris while emphasizing Trump’s primary claim: that he was uniquely equipped to curb inflation and ease the cost of living.

Fast forward two years, and elevated prices at the pump and the supermarket continue to strain family finances, making living costs the dominant concern for the electorate. 

The disparity between his promises to lower costs and the daily reality for shoppers has emerged as a critical weakness for the Republican Party leading into November's midterm elections.

According to Reuters/Ipsos polling, voters currently favor Democrats over Republicans by a slim margin on economic stewardship, marking the first time in almost ten years that Democrats have held this advantage.

Sheila Carney, a 68-year-old Trump voter, voiced her frustration with a curse word while loading $70 worth of groceries into her trunk near Trump's Bedminster facility. The haul was minimal, consisting of a bit of meat, laundry detergent and a 12-pack of iced tea.

For Carney, that checkout total demonstrated that the cost-of-living struggles Trump has on occasion brushed off as a Democratic "hoax" are very real for working families.

"This is real. He can say it's not, but it is," said Carney, a hospital administration assistant who has postponed her retirement to help clear her son's student loan debt. "He hasn't brought anything down."

An examination by Reuters covering 26 food categories monitored by the Bureau of Labor Statistics—and displayed during Trump’s Bedminster presentation—shows that prices have increased by 3.4% during the initial 19 months of his second term.

While that rate is under one-fourth of the increase registered over the equivalent stretch of former President Joe Biden’s term, it misses Trump’s goal of bringing prices down, as sharp price surges for beef, coffee and apples have outweighed price reductions in goods like butter and eggs.

A White House official cited figures released Wednesday showing minimal growth in U.S. consumer prices from June to July as proof that inflationary pressure is stabilizing.

"The July CPI report is further proof that President Trump’s long-term agenda is delivering: prescription drug and auto insurance costs continue to fall, real wages are rising, and beef prices have cooled while other household essentials like eggs, poultry, and dairy remain low," the official said.

Carney, a registered Republican, noted that elevated supermarket and fuel costs stemming from the conflict with Iran have driven her toward enough disillusionment that she may skip the upcoming midterms, mirroring broader polling trends that show weaker voter enthusiasm among Republicans compared to Democrats.

Carney was among 17 independent and Republican voters surveyed by Reuters in New Jersey's 7th Congressional District, a competitive area encompassing Bedminster where turnout among undecided voters could decide the outcome. The contest features Republican incumbent Tom Kean against Democratic challenger Rebecca Bennett, who has made economic frustration a centerpiece of her campaign.

Over half of those surveyed indicated they were undecided or leaning toward Bennett. Although food inflation was a major concern, grievances regarding Kean frequently focused on his multi-month absence from public appearances earlier in the year, an absence he linked to depression.

These economic perspectives align with comments from other Trump supporters interviewed in recent months who, despite backing the president, report that ongoing financial strain has weakened their motivation to turn out in November. Such hesitation creates an added headwind for Republicans and puts greater pressure on their voter mobilization efforts.

Francesco Trebbi, a professor of public policy at the University of California, Berkeley, recently co-authored a study demonstrating that Trump received higher support during the 2024 election in counties where inflation overtook wage gains, undercutting consumer buying power.

Because real wage growth remains sluggish and behind overall economic expansion, Trebbi suggested that dynamic could invert this November.

"I expect the same anti-incumbent shift to happen in 2026, this time possibly weakening Republicans," he said, noting that weekly grocery trips serve as a "psychologically salient" reminder of household budget constraints. "Each time one does it, it is the equivalent of a campaign ad against the incumbent."

Presidents have limited influence over inflation, which stems from complex economic variables and is primarily managed by the Federal Reserve. A significant portion of Republicans remain inclined to grant Trump leeway, even as tariff policies and the military conflict in Iran add upward pressure to prices.

Bonnie Chandler, 64, intends to back Kean, and said she believes some companies are intentionally maintaining high prices to damage Trump politically. She said the rise of progressive figures within the Democratic Party rules out supporting Democratic nominees.

"I'm going to vote Republican. I'm not a woke person. I'm not a communist. I'm not a socialist," she said.

Lauren DeGirolamo, a 34-year-old Trump voter, noted that priorities like border security and education carry greater weight for her than food costs, which she considers to have leveled off under Trump following sharp rises under the Biden administration.

"I feel grocery prices are pretty much at level with where they were during Biden. I know some of the key things that I look for - eggs - have gone down," she said, confirming her plan to vote Republican in November.

Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics indicates egg prices have dropped almost 40% under Trump, marking a market stabilization after avian flu outbreaks drove a sharp price hike that originated during the Biden presidency. Eggs are one of six categories out of 26 to experience price drops since 2025, alongside bacon, butter, and cooking fats and oils.

However, the majority of the products featured during Trump’s Bedminster showcase have grown more expensive, several by substantial margins. Raw beef has surged 19.2%, fresh fish and seafood 8.6%, apples 14%, and coffee roughly 23%.

A Reuters/Ipsos survey completed earlier this month revealed that Trump's net approval rating on managing the cost of living stood at -47%, down sharply from -6% when his term began. This marks his lowest score by a broad margin, far behind his standing on the general economy (-35%) and immigration (-16%).

Bennett told Reuters that, if victorious, her priorities would include reversing Trump's tariffs, seeking an end to the Iran conflict, and restoring food stamp funding to assist households struggling with grocery bills.

The challenge is personal, according to Bennett, a military veteran and married mother of two daughters. 

"This is not an abstract concept to me," she said. "For example, beef is very expensive, so we don't buy beef anymore."

Whether Kean—whose campaign team did not reply to inquiries for comment—can retain his district could depend on voters like Margaret Derkach, a traditional Republican leaning voter who is contemplating changing her ballot if financial burdens do not ease.

"The cost of living, as far as homes, apartments and food - the necessities - they have gone up. It's shocking, shocking," said Derkach, 84, speaking after a trip to discount supermarket Aldi.

While acknowledging that Trump "inherited a mess" from Biden, Derkach added, "I am undecided right now. I have to see."
news.summary: Most of the items Trump displayed at Bedminster are now pricier, some by a lot

news.title: Hard-boiled politics: AOC’s egg-freezing vids will lure older female voters to her prez bid: pollsters
news.text:
“Squad” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez’s extraordinarily public social media posts about freezing her eggs are nothing more than hard-boiled politics, critics told The Post.

The 36-year-old socialist lawmaker’s dramatic videos about her fertility treatments appeal to a critical slice of voters — women aged 35-49 – who could hold the key to a 2028 presidential run.

“It is her way to move into the . . . older women, rather than just the young under-34-year-olds,” said Andrew Smith, who runs the Survey Center at the University of New Hampshire.

The 35-49 female demographic is important include those who “are hearing that biological clock ticking more loudly,” he added. 

Last week, an overalls-clad AOC laid out the “ingredients” to jab her stomach on her East Elmhurst kitchen counter in one of a series of Instagram videos for her 9.7 million followers.

“Welcome to my cooking show, today we’re making eggs,” she quipped. 

“Don’t be weird about this, even though I know all of you will be,” she cautioned, acknowledging she was cracking political norms on her initial video. She stressed the financial toll of saving up for treatments, then said she shopped around and will pay $8,000-$9,000 for treatments.

Conservative critics immediately pounced.

“AOC is freezing her eggs at 36 because she wants to try to ‘relate’ to women when she runs for President in 2028,” wrote conservative activist Laura Loomer on X. 

“She knows freezing eggs at 36 when you’ve been engaged for 4 years is a lost cause. So she wants a sob story about infertility when she does decide to run for president,” she scoffed. 

The videos kicked off immediate speculation that AOC had split with her longtime beau Riley Roberts, which the socialist lawmaker did not deny.

AOC’s unusual choice to administer shots to herself on camera comes as Pew polling shows IVF is a winning political issue, with 79% of Dems and 63% of Republicans saying access to it is a good thing.

“This is something that her willingness to talk about will endear her to women,” said former CNN political reporter and independent political commentator Chris Cillizza.

 “The decision to announce it publicly suggests to me that she can reap the political benefits from it. I’d be surprised at this point if she did not run for president in 2028.”

“There are no coincidences in politics,” he added, noting she went on a Sunday show, where she knew she would be asked about her 2028 intentions, for the first time in almost two years, the morning after breaking the egg news on Instagram.

Fellow Dems dismissed the notion of an ulterior motive, cheering the ‘egg-cellent’ decision.

“I love seeing more people take ownership over their lives to make the decisions that are right for them – whether it’s through egg freezing, IVF, or something else,” Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.) told The Post. “Sharing our personal journeys is the first step to normalizing these experiences about fertility and reproductive health and help get better policies to support people.” 

The share of childless women increased in every demographic except women ages 45 to 50, according to Census Bureau data. In 2024, 91 million women voted, compared to 83 million men, according to the League of Women Voters – and the largest group of voters was women age 45-64. 

AOC already cleans up among young voters, winning 43% of those under 34 according to a UNH poll of 1,500 state residents out last month.

But she gets just 18% of those 35-49, a cohort who turn out to vote in national elections far more than the younger crowd.

Rival Pete Buttigieg, the former secretary of transportation whose late father was a prominent Marxist historian, beats her among the group, getting 24%. Buttigieg gets 27% support among women of all age groups – compared to 16% for AOC.

Buttigieg led that poll with 19% of the vote, followed by California Gov. Gavin Newsom at 15% and Ocasio-Cortez right behind at 14%.

AOC is already polling well in the battlegrounds and routinely rates among the top four Democratic candidates nationally, with a massive grassroots fundraising base and options to seek higher office in 2028. Appealing to the soccer mom/IVF crowd could be her key to the Oval Office, some suggest.

“It could be her time. She’s a real force of nature,” said Ed Rollins, who ran Ronald Reagan’s 1984 campaign. “She’s a smart politician. From the get-go she has always built a political base and expanded that base.”

Even if the purported stunt expands her base, 2024 could be a cautionary tale.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris staked much of her campaign on working to restore Roe v. Wade and ride a female backlash to victory. But she ended up losing ground among every slice of female voters to Donald Trump compared to 2020, other than women over 65.
news.summary: There are hard-boiled politics at play in AOC's IVF treatment, and there may be a sunny upside for the candidate sharing to her millions of followers online.
