news.title: Trump’s prosecutors investigate firm that was co-owned by daughter of judge in president’s hush-money trial: report
news.text:
Federal prosecutors in Chicago have been investigating Authentic Campaigns Inc., a Democratic fundraising firm once co-owned by the daughter of the judge who oversaw President Donald Trump’s New York hush-money trial, according to court filings and people familiar with the inquiry, The New York Times reported.

Last August, the U.S. attorney’s office in Chicago subpoenaed the firm for a wide range of internal communications with major Democratic clients as part of a federal investigation into whether its work involved improper conduct or potential violations of federal law.

Clients allegedly include former Vice President Kamala Harris, former President Joe Biden, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the Democratic National Committee, according to a grand jury subpoena reviewed by the Times.

Loren Merchan, the daughter of Manhattan Supreme Court Justice Juan Merchan, served as a vice president at Authentic Campaigns until late 2024 and was also named in the federal investigation. Trump and his allies have repeatedly targeted the Merchan family, accusing the judge of bias against Trump without evidence and claiming his daughter could have financially benefited from the case.

Trump’s hush-money trial ended in May 2024 with his conviction on 34 felony counts. He was accused of falsifying business records to conceal a $130,000 payment to porn star Stormy Daniels, who said she had an affair with Trump and threatened to make the story public during his 2016 presidential campaign.

Authentic Campaigns fought the subpoena through its legal team, which included former Manhattan U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara. 

After negotiations, prosecutors narrowed their request, focusing on a $468 payment from Harris’ presidential campaign and on emails exchanged between Loren Merchan and her father, according to people familiar with the investigation who spoke to the Times anonymously because the investigation is ongoing.

The current status of the investigation remains unclear. Prosecutors have not issued any additional subpoenas to Loren Merchan, Authentic Campaigns founder Michael Nellis, or other individuals, suggesting that authorities are not actively pursuing criminal charges at this time, sources told the Times. 

The Independent has contacted Authentic Campaigns and the Department of Justice for comment. 

The investigation is the latest sign that federal prosecutors, once largely insulated from politics, are increasingly being pulled into Trump’s efforts to go after his political opponents.

Trump’s attacks on Juan Merchan began around his April 2023 arraignment in the hush-money case, when he called the judge partisan, claiming on Truth Social that Merchan “hates me” and that he “must be changed.”

The attacks intensified in March 2024, after Merchan set a trial date and issued a limited gag order. Trump accused Merchan, without evidence of favoring his daughter’s Democratic political consulting interests without evidence. He called the order “illegal” and “un-American,” claiming it violated his First Amendment rights and was part of a broader effort by Democrats to weaponize law enforcement.

During the hush money trial, Trump continued attacking Merchan and violating the gag order, prompting the judge to expand the order to cover family members and hold Trump in criminal contempt of court.
news.summary: Trump and his allies have repeatedly attacked the Merchans, baselessly claiming the judge was biased and his daughter profited from his hush-money trial

news.title: Kamala Harris Snubbed as Rising Democrat Rejects Endorsement
news.text:
Mary Peltola’s Alaska Senate campaign is making one thing clear: it does not want Kamala Harris’s backing to become part of its 2026 political story.

Peltola, who is seeking one of Alaska’s two US Senate seats in November’s midterm elections, moved quickly to create distance after Harris promoted her candidacy in a recent fundraising email.

‘Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 — her focus is and always will be Alaska,’ a campaign spokesperson told The New York Times.

The aide also said Peltola had not signed off on Harris’s message, which appeared in a fundraising appeal declaring: ‘If there’s anyone who can flip Alaska and secure the Senate majority for Democrats — it’s Mary.’

Harris’s support may carry complications in Alaska, a state she lost by 14 points during the 2024 presidential race.

Republicans have already seized on the endorsement, hoping to turn Harris’s poor performance in the state into a political liability for Peltola’s Senate campaign.

Nick Puglia, a spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, argued that Peltola had worked ‘hand in hand with Kamala Harris to put Alaska last,’ adding that Harris’s support therefore came as no surprise.

Puglia was referring to Peltola’s prior stint in Congress, as US Representative for Alaska-at-large between 2022 and 2025, when Joe Biden was president and Harris was his deputy. 

Rebecca Himschoot, an Alaska state lawmaker elected as an Independent, branded Harris’s endorsement of Peltola ‘really dumb.’

She told The Times: ‘She’s riding Mary Peltola’s coattails. 

‘And she’s not even running for anything that anyone knows of yet, and didn’t do well here to begin with.’

Harris is said to have privately hinted that she will run for president again in 2028, although few Democrats welcome the prospect of a repeat of a campaign that handed Donald Trump his second White House term.

Peltola did not endorse Harris’s presidential campaign and has positioned herself as a centrist Democrat, who is campaigning on a platform of ‘fish, family and freedom.’ 

Polls show that Peltola stands a strong chance of becoming Alaska’s first Democrat senator since 2014.

Sixteen candidates – seven Republican, three Democrats, three Independents, a Libertarian, a Green and a member of the Alaska party – will all compete in the same primary as part of state election rules.

The four candidates who win the most seats will then advance to a general election.

Ten of the 11 polls forecasting the result have Peltola as a winner, with a New York Times/Siena poll predicting Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan will hold onto his seat.

Confusingly, another Republican called Daniel J. Sullivan is running as a Republican for the same seat.

That has sparked fears among the GOP that flummoxed voters will mix the two men up, and limit Dan S’s chance of holding onto his seat. 

Alaska leans conservative but its voters have an independent streak. 

Republican Lisa Murkowski, the state’s other US Senator, backed Peltola in her previous bids for the House of Representatives, despite the two women belonging to rival parties. 

Murkowski has backed Dan S. Sullivan for this year’s senate race. 

President Trump’s increasingly unpopular war in Iran is seen as a gift to Peltola’s campaign and could ultimately help her flip the seat.

news.title: Trump’s 2024 grocery photo op now haunts Republicans in the midterms
news.text:
BEDMINSTER, New Jersey - Two years after Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump staged a New Jersey press conference flanked by grocery staples to spotlight inflation under Democrats, food prices are still rising despite his pledge to bring them down.

The gap between promise and reality now looms as a vulnerability for Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Standing between tables piled high with fruit, beef, cereal, milk and other household staples at his Bedminster golf club on Aug 15, 2024, Trump blamed the Biden administration for sharp increases in groceries.

The spectacle, complete with charts showing higher prices, was aimed at undercutting the Democratic nominee, Kamala Harris, and highlighted Trump’s central promise: he alone could tame inflation and lower the cost of living.

Two years on, higher petrol and grocery prices are squeezing household budgets and turning the cost of living into the top issue for American voters.

Voters now give Democrats a slight edge over Republicans in who they view as better stewards of the economy for the first time in nearly a decade, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.

Sheila Carney, a 68-year-old Trump voter, punctuated her frustration with an expletive as she unloaded US$70 (S$89.57) worth of groceries into her car outside a supermarket not far from Trump’s Bedminster club.

The haul was modest: some meat, detergent and a 12-pack of iced tea.

For Carney, the receipt was evidence that the affordability concerns Trump has sometimes dismissed as a Democratic “hoax” remain a daily burden for many Americans.

“This is real. He can say it’s not, but it is,” said Carney, a hospital administration assistant who has delayed retirement while helping pay off her son’s student loans. “He hasn’t brought anything down.”

A Reuters analysis of 26 grocery categories tracked by the Bureau of Labour Statistics and featured in Trump’s Bedminster display found prices have risen 3.4 per cent in the first 19 months of his second term.

That’s less than a quarter of the pace recorded at the same point in former President Joe Biden’s term, but still falls short of Trump’s pledge to lower prices, as surges in coffee, beef and apples have more than offset declines in items including eggs and butter.

A White House official pointed to data on Aug 13 that showed US consumer prices barely increased in July from the month before as evidence that inflation is under control.

“The July CPI report is further proof that President Trump’s long-term agenda is delivering: prescription drug and auto insurance costs continue to fall, real wages are rising, and beef prices have cooled while other household essentials like eggs, poultry, and dairy remain low,” the official said.

Lack of enthusiasm

A registered Republican, Carney said high grocery and petrol prices due to the Iran war were among the reasons she had grown disillusioned enough to consider sitting out the midterms, underscoring recent polling suggesting Republicans are less enthusiastic about voting than Democrats.

Carney was one of 17 Republicans and independents Reuters interviewed in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District, a battleground that includes Bedminster and where swing voters and turnout could prove decisive.

The race pits Republican incumbent Tom Kean against Democrat Rebecca Bennett, who has sought to capitalise on voters’ frustration over the cost of living.

More than half of those interviewed said they were either undecided or leaning toward Bennett.

While grocery prices weighed heavily on many voters, complaints about Kean more often centred on his months-long disappearance from public view earlier in 2026, which he later attributed to depression.

Their views on the economy mirror those of other Trump supporters Reuters has interviewed in recent months who, despite standing by the president, say financial pressures have dampened their enthusiasm for voting in November.

That ambivalence presents another potential challenge for Republicans and raises the stakes for the party’s get-out-the-vote operation.

Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley, recently co-authored research finding that Trump drew stronger support in the 2024 election in counties where inflation outpaced income growth, eroding households’ purchasing power.

With real wages rising only marginally and lagging the pace of broader economic growth, Trebbi said it is likely that pattern will reverse in November.

“I expect the same anti-incumbent shift to happen in 2026, this time possibly weakening Republicans,” he said, describing grocery shopping as a “psychologically salient” reminder of the squeeze on household finances.

“Each time one does it, it is the equivalent of a campaign ad against the incumbent.”

Trump support

To be sure, presidents have limited influence over inflation, which is driven by a range of factors and more directly addressed by the Federal Reserve.

And many Republicans appear willing to give Trump the benefit of the doubt, even as his tariffs and the Iran war have contributed to rising prices.

Bonnie Chandler, 64, plans to vote for Kean, saying she believed some companies were keeping prices elevated to make Trump look bad and that the growing influence of the Democratic Party’s progressive faction left her unwilling to consider its candidates.

“I’m going to vote Republican. I’m not a woke person. I’m not a communist. I’m not a socialist,” she said.

Lauren DeGirolamo, a 34-year-old Trump voter, said issues such as education and border security mattered more to her than grocery prices, which she believes have stabilized under Trump following steep increases during the Biden administration.

“I feel grocery prices are pretty much at level with where they were during Biden. I know some of the key things that I look for - eggs - have gone down,” she said, adding that she intended to vote for Republican candidates in November.

According to BLS data, egg prices have fallen nearly 40 per cent under Trump, reflecting a market correction after avian flu-driven shortages triggered a surge that began during Biden’s presidency.

Eggs are among six of the 26 categories showing falls since 2025, along with butter, bacon, and cooking fats and oils.

Yet most of the items Trump displayed at Bedminster are now pricier, some by a lot. Uncooked beef has jumped 19.2 per cent, fresh fish and seafood 8.6 per cent, apples 14 per cent, and coffee nearly 23 per cent.

Hitting close to home

A Reuters/Ipsos poll that concluded earlier in August found Trump’s net approval rating on his handling of the cost of living was at -47 per cent, down from -6 per cent at the start of his term.

It is his weakest issue by a wide margin, trailing his ratings on the economy (-35 per cent) and immigration (-16 per cent).

Bennett told Reuters that if elected she would seek to undo Trump’s tariffs, rein in the Iran war, and restore food stamp benefits to help families struggling to afford groceries.

The issue hits close to home, said Bennett, a military veteran and married mother of two daughters.

“This is not an abstract concept to me,” she said. “For example, beef is very expensive, so we don’t buy beef anymore.”

Whether Kean, whose campaign did not respond to requests for comment, can hold on to his seat may depend on voters like Margaret Derkach, who typically votes Republican but is now considering switching her vote if economic conditions don’t improve.

“The cost of living, as far as homes, apartments and food - the necessities - they have gone up. It’s shocking, shocking,” said Derkach, 84, after shopping at discount grocer Aldi.

Though she said Trump “inherited a mess” from Biden, Derkach added, “I am undecided right now. I have to see.” REUTERS

news.title: Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs again refuses in-person face-off against GOP opponent
news.text:
Her campaign says she has participated in more than 100 open-press events and interviews this year and argues that meeting voters directly is more valuable than appearing on a stage designed for “short soundbites and political theater.” Biggs, 67, has seized on the refusal, repeatedly challenging Hobbs to debate and making her absence itself part of his campaign message.

The standoff echoes a developing dynamic in California, Arizona’s behemoth neighbor to the west. There, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton has repeatedly pressed Democratic front-runner Xavier Becerra to debate him. Together, the races raise a larger question about whether incumbents and front-runners increasingly calculate that debates offer more risk than reward, particularly when campaigns can communicate directly to voters through television, digital, and social media.

For incumbents, debates can do more harm than good

The shift is not entirely new. President Donald Trump helped demonstrate it in 2024. His lone debate against Joe Biden, both his successor and predecessor, forced the Democratic incumbent from the race. In the June 27 debate, put on by CNN, the then-president delivered a halting performance with a raspy voice, struggling with multiple stumbles and lost trains of thought. Following weeks of sharp drops in the polls and mounting pressure from Democratic leaders, Biden withdrew from the race against Trump. His vice president, Kamala Harris, stepped in as the Democratic nominee but lost to Trump in November, giving him a second, nonconsecutive term.

Trump, during that lone debate with Biden, was relatively subdued, at least by his standards. But Trump’s long history of debate participation, or lack thereof, has led candidates in both parties to rethink the wisdom of participating at all. Going back to Trump’s 2016 Republican primary bid, he beat a slew of establishment politicians by participating in debates only when he felt like it.

“Trump changed the calculus on debates,” Democratic strategist Nick Smith told the Washington Examiner. “Period. He skipped every Republican primary debate, dominated the media anyway, and cruised to the nomination. He proved that refusing to debate is no longer the political death knell it once was.”

Hobbs, Smith noted, has already tested the strategy herself.

“She refused to debate Kari Lake, took a beating for it, and still won by 17,117 votes,” he said. “And Lake wasn’t starved for attention — she had Trump and national media behind her.”

An AARP poll conducted in late July found Hobbs leading Biggs 52%-44%.

“So if I’m Hobbs and I’m leading Biggs 52%-44%, I don’t debate,” Smith said. “Why give the guy who’s 8 points down a free shot at changing the race?”

That calculation could change if the race tightens.

“If the economy, wars, or political environment move against her and that lead shrinks to 2 points, ask me again,” Smith said. “Debates aren’t dead. The idea that you have to debate is. Trump killed that rule.”

But Aaron Kall, director of debate at the University of Michigan, said they remain an important political norm.

“They are an excellent demonstration of political skills that are needed for success in public office,” Kall told the Washington Examiner, citing public speaking, critical thinking, answering questions candidates have not previously considered, thinking on their feet, and operating under pressure. Kall argued debates serve as a rare test of how candidates respond to unscripted questions and pressure.

Garry South, a veteran California Democratic strategist, said the electoral impact of gubernatorial debates is nevertheless often overstated.

“The overwhelming majority of voters don’t spend an hour or 90 minutes of their time watching debates for offices other than president,” South told the Washington Examiner. “Except in cases where one candidate has a complete meltdown, like Biden in ’24, debates are almost never as decisive or determinative as the candidate who is behind talks themselves into believing.”

Biggs has to turn the refusal into a liability

Republican strategist Jeff Burton called debates in today’s climate “just another campaign tactic.”

“If I were advising Gov. Hobbs, I’d tell her to do whatever helps her win,” said Burton, who previously was deputy executive director of the National Republican Congressional Committee. “There’s no extra credit in politics, and the burden is on Andy Biggs to convince voters she’s avoiding him because she can’t defend her record. There’s no upside to her to commit to a debate right now.”

But Republican strategist Mike Ricci, a partner at Seven Letter who was former Maryland Gov. Larry Hogan’s communications director, said the strategic advantage for incumbents does not necessarily mean they should refuse to debate altogether.

“Start with the structural reality: incumbent governors are incredibly difficult to knock off,” Ricci said. “That alone shapes the debate calculus. Challengers need the debates more, while incumbents want to avoid putting them on equal footing or creating opportunities for gaffes or viral moments that can turn into TV ads.”

Ricci said challengers can turn an incumbent’s refusal into a campaign issue — if they do it effectively.

“They have to make the refusal politically damaging without sounding like they’re whining or getting pulled off message,” he told the Washington Examiner. “It will all sound like inside baseball to voters unless the refusal reinforces something they already suspect, that a governor is inaccessible, out of touch, or acting like the rules don’t apply to them.”

He added that, given how close her race was last time, “her team has plenty of reason to view a debate as high risk and low reward.” Still, Ricci said he would advise an incumbent to agree to at least one debate under controlled conditions.

Reach of local media adds to the equation 

The decline of local media may also be changing the incentives around debates.

Fewer local outlets can force candidates into sustained public exchanges, while campaigns increasingly have their own platforms to reach voters.

“It’s tough to see this pendulum swinging back, especially with local and statewide campaigns increasingly looking like federal races, with fewer people watching debates, more hostility toward the outlets that host them, and more candidates choosing social media and other controlled platforms where they can plausibly argue they reach more people,” Ricci said.

Rodd McLeod, a Phoenix-based Democratic strategist, argues the question should be framed differently.

The issue is not whether voters are being denied the opportunity to watch candidates debate each other, but whether they are being denied opportunities to see candidates “get challenged, or take tough questions,” he told the Washington Examiner.

Presidential debates still attract large audiences, but gubernatorial debates are different. The first and only Republican gubernatorial primary debate in Arizona this year, which included Biggs and Rep. David Schweikert (R-AZ), drew only a fraction of the state’s electorate online. McLeod argues that campaigns are increasingly operating through short-form video, podcasts, and direct-to-voter communication.

“The people who attend in-person debates and forums already know who they are voting for,” he said. “Televised debates offer the public a look at the candidates but get skimpy viewership.”

For Hobbs, the decision to avoid a debate may therefore be less about fear of Biggs than whether the event would provide enough benefit to justify the risk.

Are debates becoming obsolete? 

Biggs’s campaign has an obvious incentive to keep pressing the issue. He has used Hobbs’s refusal as a recurring line of attack, arguing that an incumbent should have to defend her record before voters. But Kall said Hobbs’s approach remains an outlier among major candidates and could eventually carry a political cost.

“Gov. Hobbs has built an anti-debate brand that has proved politically effective and astute to date,” Kall said. “She clearly believes the potential upside from debating her opponents is outweighed by what could happen: negative reviews, a major disqualifying gaffe, etc.”

So far, that calculation has worked. But Kall said he would advise Hobbs to debate Biggs, particularly because the Republican is not especially known as an astute political debater. Hobbs’s refusal also stands out compared with other gubernatorial candidates, Kall said.

PROGRESSIVES WANT TO SKIRT PAST THEIR ‘WOKE’ PASTS. CENTRISTS WON’T LET THEM

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has avoided debates in the past but is expected to debate Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico. At the same time, Becerra has participated in numerous California gubernatorial debates ahead of the June 2 all-party primary, events that included Hilton. Becerra has said he will eventually debate Hilton ahead of Election Day, Nov. 3. That creates a familiar political paradox: The candidate who most wants a debate is often the candidate who needs it most, while the candidate who has the most to lose can decline.

Whether the strategy carries a political cost may ultimately depend on Biggs. If he can convince voters that Hobbs’s refusal reflects an unwillingness to defend her record, it could become a liability. If voters barely notice, Hobbs may have avoided the downside of a debate without sacrificing much in return.

Barnini Chakraborty (@Barnini) is a senior political reporter at the Washington Examiner.

Katie Hobbs (D-AZ) is once again refusing to debate a Republican challenger, reviving a question that could become increasingly difficult for incumbent governors to avoid: Can they get away with avoiding a face-off against their opponent, a staple of modern statewide campaigns? Hobbs says she won’t debate Rep. Andy Biggs (R-AZ), the GOP gubernatorial […]

news.title: Maybe Americans are too hard on Congress
news.text:
There is plenty to be dissatisfied about. Gas prices are high, as are the interest rates on 30-year mortgages and car loans. There has been a spate of scandals in the first six months of this year.

The public perusing the news will read that Rep. Max Miller (R-OH) allegedly assaulted his wife and injured his toddler. (He emphatically denies the allegations.) John and Jane Q Public also will see reports detailing creepy behavior by Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-NC), Rep. Cory Mills (R-FL), and former legislators Tony Gonzales, a Texas Republican, and Eric Swalwell, a California Democrat. They will also learn that former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, a Florida Democrat who misused $5 million in federal funds and quit Congress to avoid being thrown out, is campaigning to rejoin the House.

And Congress has not had an especially productive year. It has passed 25 substantive laws and a couple of resolutions to disapprove of regulations. It has not, however, made substantial progress toward enacting the 12 annual spending bills. One of the last things senators did before returning home to campaign was to vote for a continuing resolution, an explicit confession that they are not going to get their work done on time.

“Funding the government is Congress’s most fundamental responsibility,” groused Taxpayers for Common Sense, a group that advocates fiscally responsible policymaking. “The Senate has yet to move a single appropriations bill out of committee. Neither chamber is close to completing all twelve bills before the fiscal year ends.”

For all there is to lament about Congress, people should not succumb to “cynicism and despair,” writes Frances Lee, Princeton professor and the author of A Case for Congress (Oklahoma University Press). Congress might be struggling, but it is still performing its three basic purposes: representation, lawmaking, and overseeing the executive branch.

Voters frequently complain that Congress is filled with lawyers and polarized elites who are out of touch with the average American. That is not a particularly accurate assessment, according to Professor Lee.

Congress’s membership is not a perfect mirror of the diverse public, but it far better reflects the people than the executive and judicial branches. The federal judiciary is staffed with individuals with advanced degrees from mostly elite universities, and the president’s cabinet mostly comprises members of one party who are disproportionately drawn from major metropolitan areas and the upper echelon of society.

Congress represents diverse local interests and the United States population broadly. Its 535 members mostly represent districts and states where they have spent much of their lives.

Yes, it has its share of individuals with law degrees (32% of representatives and 47% of senators), which is unsurprising since Congress is a law-making institution. Mostly, though, Congress is made up of folks who are not lawyers: doctors, ministers, scientists, engineers, teachers, farmers, and restaurateurs, to name just several occupations. In terms of race, religion, gender, and class, Congress today is more representative of America than it ever has been. And, yes, like the United States itself, Congress has sleazebags and charlatans — sent there by voters.

Politically, Professor Lee points out, Congress’s partisan split well reflects the partisan split among people. “In the 2024 election, for example, Kamala Harris won 48% of the national popular vote. That year, Democrats won 49% of House seats and 47% of Senate seats. In the 2020 elections, President Biden won 51% of the national popular vote; Democrats won 51% of House seats and 50% of Senate seats.” For all the gerrymandering, neither party is overrepresented in Congress. Like the American public, Congress has wild-eyed leftists, barking right-wingers, and people in-between. 

Congress is a venue where unconventional and unpopular public views can be expressed. During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, it was legislators — not judges or agency administrators — who questioned the executive branch’s claims about the origins of the virus and the wisdom of school lockdowns. Legislators have given speeches about UFOs and other topics deemed fringe by elites.

Although Washington gives the appearance of gridlock, Congress continues to make laws. “As gauged by sheer volume,” Professor Lee writes, “recent Congresses have passed just as much legislation as Congresses of the 1970s and 1980s.” Despite partisan polarization, the laws that get made usually are not passed on party lines. Thanks to the filibuster and the internal divisions within the two parties, they are enacted by coalitions and draw broad support from both parties. On average, a new law is passed by 78 senators (78% of the chamber) and 338 House members (77.7% of the chamber).

Voters are not wrong in thinking that presidents whose party controls both the Senate and House are subjected to less rigorous oversight. Politics is a team sport. Nevertheless, no president can evade oversight entirely. Congress’s constitutional power over lawmaking and revenue-raising guarantees give legislators the power to nudge or curb the executive branch. For example, this magazine reported on the GOP-majority Congress resisting President Donald Trump’s effort to take control of the Library of Congress. House Republicans not only rebuffed the president, but they also passed a bill to thwart any future president from seizing the library.

Individual legislators, Professor Lee explains, can express their criticism of a president and his administration on the floor of Congress or to the media or directly to voters. The airing of grievances is a key feature of a legislature and can provide feedback to a president and his appointees. Federal bureaucracies are prone to developing insular and technocratic cultures. Carping from Congress calls out the narrow groupthink in agencies that leads to taxpayers’ dollars being spent on things such as drag shows in Ecuador.

IRAN THROWS WRENCH INTO HORMUZ DEAL WITH NEW LIST OF DEMANDS TO US

None of this is to deny that Congress has problems. Too many members forget their constitutional roles as lawmakers and behave like reality-television contestants or social media influencers. The gratuitous partisanship and toxic rhetoric turn off many people and sadly feed the extremist trolls amongst us.

Yet Professor Lee is right: we should value Congress more than we do. “[W]e would be worse off without the Congress.” A government without a representative assembly is a tyranny. And in this polarized, contentious era we need a legislative branch that channels the clashing interests and perspectives and forces them to talk and bargain with one another before policy gets made that binds us all.

news.title: Karoline Leavitt knew exactly what she was doing
news.text:
Karoline Leavitt, the outgoing White House press secretary, is the embodiment of a presidency unleashed, with little regard for truth or transparency.

Consider: In her first briefing as White House press secretary, Leavitt defended the Trump administration’s freeze on federal grants by pointing to a particular line item as “preposterous” — $50 million to fund condoms in Gaza. When I queried Leavitt about the source of her statistic, she responded by sending a Fox News article that initially just quoted her own statement. When I looked into the sum, I found that the U.S. Agency for International Development had spent $119 million over six years to buy condoms to prevent the spread of HIV/AIDS, making the claim implausible. Eventually, it also became clear the administration had mixed up the Hamas-controlled Gaza Strip with the Gaza province of Mozambique (though even then, none of that money was spent on condoms).

Under Trump, the role of the White House press secretary has been diminished almost to the point of meaninglessness.

Leavitt never admitted she was wrong. And, despite the fact checks, Trump doubled down — and claimed the figure was $100 million.

Over three decades working in Washington, I have dealt with 20 White House press secretaries, from Dee Dee Myers, the first woman to hold the job, to Leavitt, the youngest person to hold the job and Trump’s fifth press secretary as president.

Reporters expect press secretaries to put the best possible gloss on an administration’s policies. But they’re also supposed to provide information that helps reporters accurately explain what the White House is doing. 

Under Trump, the role of the White House press secretary has been diminished almost to the point of meaninglessness. Trump often acts as his own spokesperson, spewing lies in constant encounters with reporters and in his frequent social media posts. In his first term, his third press secretary, Stephanie Grisham, never even held a formal press briefing. Leavitt, for her part, has shamelessly echoed the president’s favorite falsehoods.

Spin is part of the job. Outright lying is not.

When I started covering the White House, during the Clinton administration, I had shifted over from focusing on tax and budget policy. I vividly recall attending my first media briefing in the White House and listening to then-Press Secretary Mike McCurry give a skillful defense of President Bill Clinton’s misbegotten Bosnia policy. I didn’t know much about the nuances and found myself nodding, thinking his explanation made sense.

Then someone asked about the federal budget. McCurry responded, and I remember shaking my head. “What BS,” I thought. “This is so misleading.”

Then I realized — once I knew more about Bosnia, I’d see how he’d been spinning on that, too. 

The best press secretaries had the confidence of the president and his inner circle, so they could speak knowledgeably about the president’s agenda. Even if they defended a problematic decision, they tried to stick as close as possible to the truth. 

As Richard Nixon’s press secretary, Ron Ziegler, discovered, there was once a price to pay for crossing the line from spin to outright falsehood. Ziegler had dismissed the Watergate break-in as a “third-rate burglary” and attacked The Washington Post for “shabby journalism” and “character assassination.”

But the stories turned out to be correct. After two of Nixon’s closest aides resigned for their involvement in the cover-up, Ziegler apologized. “Mistakes were made during this period,” Ziegler said. “I was overenthusiastic.”

He acknowledged the Post’s Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein “have vigorously pursued this story and they deserve the credit and are receiving the credit for it. When we’re wrong, we’re wrong, and I would have to say I was in that case and other cases.”

Ziegler understood something that once seemed fundamental to the job: A press secretary without credibility was of little use to the president.

Under Trump, however, no one offers a mea culpa. The tone was set the day after Trump’s first inauguration, when Trump ordered his first press secretary, Sean Spicer, to claim that “his was the largest audience to ever witness an inauguration — period — both in person and around the globe.” 

Attendees line the National Mall as they watch ceremonies to swear in Donald Trump on Inauguration Day on Jan. 20, 2017, in Washington, DC.

Spicer lashed out at reporters who accurately reported that the crowd for Trump was smaller than that for Barack Obama. He offered a series of easily disproven claims to back up his nonsense, such as that this was the first time that floor coverings were used on the National Mall.

Trump never dropped the crowd claim. Running for re-election in 2020, he bragged that “we had the largest audience anywhere in the world.” He even accused the media of showing photos from “five or six hours” before he started speaking.

Spicer’s credibility with the press was destroyed almost immediately. He was gone within six months, replaced by Sarah Huckabee Sanders — now the governor of Arkansas — who was more skilled at dissembling.

On several occasions, for example, Sanders told reporters that “countless” FBI agents had told her that they were thankful Trump had fired FBI Director James Comey. But when she was interviewed by Special Counsel Robert Mueller, she admitted this was “a comment she made ‘in the heat of the moment’ that was not founded on anything.” She described the lie as a “slip of the tongue.” 

Funny how her tongue kept slipping. Over time, she all but ended the daily briefing, with gaps of more than a month as Trump seized the megaphone for himself. 

Grisham, the press secretary who avoided the briefing room, later became a Trump critic and endorsed Kamala Harris in 2024. Addressing the Democratic National Convention that year, Grisham said, “I never held a White House briefing because, unlike my boss, I never wanted to stand at that podium and lie.”

Fast-forward to Leavitt and Trump’s second term. Except when she was on maternity leave, Leavitt kept to a regular schedule of at least one to two briefings a week, leaving no doubt she was a true believer in Trump. In a social media post on her resignation, Trump called her “one of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office.” 

Press secretaries once worried that getting caught in a lie would destroy their credibility. In Trump’s White House, there is apparently no penalty for having none.
news.author: Ja’han Jones

news.title: Donald Trump’s Approval Rating Changes With Middle-Aged Americans
news.text: Middle-aged Americans are souring on President Donald Trump, according to the latest polls by The Economist/YouGov, as these voters grow more concerned about the future of Social Security and Medicare and the rising cost of living, experts say. The most recent poll, conducted between August 7 and 10 among 1,589 U.S. adults, shows that Trump's net approval rating among Americans aged 45 to 64—a combination of Gen Xers and younger baby boomers—has plummeted to -25, with 60 percent disapproving of the way he is handling the job and 35 percent approving. That is a significant drop from earlier this summer. A survey conducted between June 5 and 8 among 1,568 U.S. adults found that the president's net approval rating was -10 among that age group, with 43 percent approving of his job performance and 53 percent disapproving. A month later, a survey conducted between July 10 and 13 found that Trump's net approval rating had fallen to -12, as 43 percent of Americans aged 45-64 approved of his handling of the presidency, while 55 percent disapproved. Trump's net approval rating has not only declined twofold among middle-aged Americans but also fallen at a faster rate than any other demographic group this summer, though it remained significantly higher than among Gen Zers and millennials. As of the latest poll, Trump's net approval rating was -41 percent among Americans aged 18 to 29 and -35 among those aged 30 to 44. Among older Americans, those over 65, the president's net approval rating was -18. "A drop that big among 45-to-64-year-olds stands out," said Craig Agranoff, an adjunct professor at Florida Atlantic University who specializes in political marketing and campaigning. "This is a large group that turns out reliably and pays close attention to pocketbook issues and retirement security," he told Newsweek. Newsweek contacted the White House for comment by email on Friday morning. The 'Sandwich Generation' Turns on Trump The latest poll's findings on the state of the economy may offer an idea of why middle-aged Americans might be growing disenchanted with the president and his administration. At 79 percent, Americans aged 45 to 64 were more likely than any other generation to say the current state of the U.S. economy was "fair" or "poor." For adults aged 18 to 29, that figure was 72 percent—the same for those over 65. While 74 percent of those aged 30 to 44 said the same. Only 19 percent of Americans aged 45 to 64 believed the economy was in an "excellent" or "good" state, which was again a lower number than any other age cohort: 24 percent for Americans aged 18 to 29, 22 percent for those aged 30 to 44, and 27 percent for those over 65. A majority of middle-aged Americans—54 percent—also believed the economy was "getting worse," with only 14 percent saying it was "getting better." Inflation was the most important issue for all age groups, with 34 percent of middle-aged Americans saying so. These figures were more or less the same through the summer. Much of middle-aged Americans' dissatisfaction and concern over the state of the U.S. economy likely comes from rising inflation since the war in Iran began on February 28, as energy prices shot through the roof. Middle-aged Americans—also known as the "sandwich generation"—are often managing competing financial responsibilities, including mortgages and housing costs, college tuition for their children, and the necessary care for their elderly parents. These financial burdens have gotten heavier over the past few years. Home price growth reported the 37th consecutive month of year-over-year increases in July, with the median sales price for an existing home at $434,100, according to data from the National Association of Realtors. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.69 percent last week, the fifth consecutive week of increases after rising from 6.43 percent to 6.66 percent over the course of July. The latest data shared by Freddie Mac on Thursday found that the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was relatively stable over the past week at 6.67 percent—still near the peaks reached after the pandemic. College expenses are rising faster than inflation, according to a new report that shows that the typical student's family spent $34,019 on college in the 2025-26 academic year, 10 percent more than a year earlier, at $30,837. The cost of taking care of an elderly parent is also rising faster than older adults' incomes and inflation, led by an almost 50 percent increase in the costs of home care and assisted living, according to a recent report from the AARP Public Policy Institute. Within this period, the cost of adult day services rose 33 percent, while nursing home costs jumped 25 percent. However, household income for those 65 and older grew 22 percent. As they approach retirement, instead of breathing a sigh of relief, middle-aged Americans are stressing over high housing and health care expenditure, weakened retirement confidence, concern over Social Security and Medicare, and tariff-related price effects. The 2026 EBRI/Greenwald Retirement Confidence Survey found that about four in five workers and seven in 10 retirees were worried that the government would make changes to the U.S. retirement system. Only about half of workers and six in 10 retirees were confident that Social Security and Medicare would continue providing benefits of equal value. This is especially relevant to people aged 45 to 64 because they are approaching the key program ages while many remain dependent on employer-based work and health coverage. Social Security can generally be claimed from age 62, Medicare eligibility generally begins at 65, and full retirement age is 67 for people born in 1960 or later. Agranoff believes that middle-aged Americans are likely being affected by growing concerns over the future of the two programs they hope to rely on in the near future. "Social Security and Medicare sit high on their list of concerns, so any sense that those programs face pressure or that costs are rising can move numbers quickly," Agranoff said. What Does This Mean for the GOP in Future Elections? Middle-aged Americans have been a strong source of support for Trump in both the 2020 and the 2024 presidential election. In 2020, 50 percent of voters in this age group voted for Trump, according to national exit polls cited by NBC News, while 49 percent backed Joe Biden. In 2024, Trump made gains with this age group—with 54 percent of voters aged 45 to 64 backing him, while 44 percent supported then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump's margin in the age group widened from +1 point to +10 points. Their shift away from Trump "matters in national elections because these voters are often decisive in the suburbs and in swing states with older working-age populations," Agranoff told Newsweek. He continued, "If the slide continues, Republicans will face a tougher map in competitive House districts and in places like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin where middle-aged turnout can tip close races." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Shakeema Edwards.
news.summary: Middle-aged Americans are souring on Trump as they face growing worries over retirement, Social Security, Medicare and inflation.

news.title: Stephen A. Smith admits Florida Rep. Byron Donalds could make him a Republican, calls him ‘the real deal’
news.text:
ESPN host Stephen A. Smith said Thursday that Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., could make him a Republican, praising the Trump-backed gubernatorial frontrunner days before Florida Republicans choose their nominee to succeed Gov. Ron DeSantis.

“And I ain’t no d— Republican. But that mean if anybody could make me one, it would be him. I’m just going to keep it a buck. I’m just letting you know,” Smith said.

“He’s the real deal. Make no mistake about it. I’ve seen him battling with Democrats. I’ve seen him battling with people on different shows, whatever. He ain’t backing up. He knows his stuff. OK? I talk to him all the time. All the time. And I ain’t got nothing bad to say about him.”

A Donalds campaign official confirmed to Fox News Digital Friday that Smith and Donalds are friends. Campaign communications director Gates McGavick said Donalds was attracting voters across demographic groups by focusing on affordability and public safety.

“Byron Donalds is drawing support from Floridians of all backgrounds because he has a clear vision to make Florida more affordable, keep Floridians safe and make sure the radical left stays out of the Sunshine State,” McGavick said.

“He is building a broad coalition that puts common sense over crazy to lead Florida into the future.”

One GOP source’s assessment provided to Fox News Digital Friday focused on President Donald Trump’s endorsement.

“Donalds is endorsed by POTUS, and we fully expect him to win the primary,” the source said.

A James Madison Institute poll released Aug. 6 placed Donalds at 49% among likely Republican primary voters, 31 points ahead of Lt. Gov. Jay Collins. 

Donalds’ campaign had raised more than $90 million while facing Collins, former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner and investor James Fishback as DeSantis withheld an endorsement of any candidate.

Smith described himself as skeptical of Democrats while pressing Donalds on Black voters’ distrust of Trump and concerns about Donalds’ close alignment with the president.

“You heard me ask that question [What have Democrats done for you?]. I ain’t apologizing for it. I’m very skeptical about them,” Smith said.

“Make no mistake about it. I mean, I’ve lost interest in them in a lot of different ways. I’ll be the first to admit it right here on the public airwaves, but I also am trying to be fair-minded when I think about this,” he added.

The comments continue Smith’s increasing openness to Republican candidates. In March, he challenged Democrats to earn Black votes rather than take them for granted. 

Days later, he told Sean Hannity that, despite being a Democrat, he would support Secretary of State Marco Rubio over prominent Democrats, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Donalds answered Smith’s question about skepticism among Black voters by urging them to assess politicians through policies and results rather than personal comfort or social media commentary.

“It’s something that I acknowledge. I would challenge Black people in America. First of all, this ain’t even about trust. It’s about verification,” Donalds said.

“We’ve had people on both sides of the aisle promise Black people everything until the cows come home. But it’s really about, ‘Are you going to verify the promises and verify what the policies actually do, or are you just going to trust it because you have comfort level with a certain politician.”

Fox News Digital reached out to Smith for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

DeSantis, who was re-elected in a landslide in 2022, is barred from running for a third term. Over the past 10 years, Florida has gone from being a swing state to being dominated by Republicans at the state and national levels.
news.summary: "He's the real deal. Make no mistake about it. I've seen him battling with Democrats," Smith said.

news.title: Is the US ready for President Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez?
news.text:
“They assume that my ambition is positional. They assume that my ambition is a title or a seat. And my ambition is way bigger than that. My ambition is to change this country.”

The words were delivered slowly, deliberately and with some steeliness by Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Her audience, crammed into the pews of Rockefeller Memorial chapel at the University of Chicago, burst into spontaneous applause. That was in May. In the three months since, the speculation around Ocasio-Cortez’s ambitions – for herself and for America – has only grown louder.

Friends and foes alike wonder if the stars are aligning for the New York congresswoman to run for US president in 2028. They point to voters raging against the machine – including the ageing Democratic party establishment – and hungry for change. They note how progressives pushing for economic justice and universal healthcare have won a string of impressive victories in mayoral elections and congressional primaries over the past year.

Then there are the opinion polls. Last month a Granite State Poll from the University of New Hampshire found Ocasio-Cortez leading a potential Democratic field in that crucial state. She has the kind of name recognition that money can’t buy, nearly 10m followers on Instagram alone and fans ranging from the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) to Nancy Pelosi, the former speaker of the House of Representatives.

As Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden showed, presidential elections have a habit of finding the right person at the right time in the right place. Ocasio-Cortez, a 36-year-old with a progressive agenda and can’t-be-taught social media smarts, could meet the moment for a nation eager for a fresh start after a decade of Trumpism.

If modern politics is about pendulum swings, it is hard to imagine anyone who better personifies a rebuke of the octogenarian Trump and his nativist “Make America great again” (Maga) movement. This week a Zogby Strategies national poll found that a generic democratic socialist candidate leads generic Maga candidate 45% to 33%.

Ashik Siddique, a co-chair of the DSA, of which Ocasio-Cortez is a member, said: “If she were to throw her hat in the ring, there would be a lot of excitement for it from members of Democratic Socialists of America. We definitely want to see a strong working class voice in the 2028 presidential primary.”

Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a run for president and her actions have done nothing to quell the notion of a campaign in stealth mode. Last year she joined her mentor, the independent senator Bernie Sanders, on a “Fighting Oligarchy” tour that drew huge crowds. More recently she has crisscrossed the country to support progressive candidates, further enhancing her national profile.

In the past week alone she made two moves that intensified political pundits’ chatter. First Ocasio-Cortez used Instagram to announce that she is freezing her eggs, a decision she described as a move to “feel more in control of my life”. She acknowledged the “political risk” in sharing personal family planning details but stated her goal is to normalise conversations about the professional and personal challenges women face. The internet quickly became awash in speculation that Ocasio-Cortez ended her relationship with and engagement to long-time partner Riley Roberts , driven by reports from Puck News and others noting she had long since stopped appearing with him in public and mentioning his name.

Then, when asked by ABC interviewer Jonathan Karl about the cultural battles of the 2020 pandemic era – including calls from some on the left to defund the police – she laughed and, quoting a New York city council ally, remarked: “Woke One was crazy” – apparently trying to draw a strategic line between hard-fought struggles for racial justice and the performative excesses of lockdown isolation that became an easy target for the right.

Unlike many would-be presidents of the time, Ocasio-Cortez does not appear to be driven by personal ego, according to those who knew her, which may prove to be her political superpower. She was a volunteer organiser for Sanders’ 2016 campaign, his first presidential run and one that built a national movement around his vision of democratic socialism, even as he lost to former secretary of state Hillary Clinton.

When she decided to run for office herself, the former bartender and waitress had virtually no money but was assisted by progressive organisations such as Brand New Congress and Justice Democrats. In 2018 she beat 10-term incumbent congressman Joe Crowley, a member of the Democratic leadership and potential future speaker, in a New York primary.

Corbin Trent, her first communications director in the House of Representatives and the co-founder of Justice Democrats, was there on the night she ousted Crowley. He recalls that the political industrial complex began trying to map her career path before the ink on the ballots was even dry.

“Primary night, she beats Joe Crowley,” he recalled. “I get phone calls from elected officials and other people and their question is, what’s next? What’s the pathway here? What’s she going to run for? What higher office would she seek? This is literally a few hours after the polls close in the primary. That’s the way DC thinks. Not, hey, what can we do with Medicare for all or this or that or any of the other things?”

As Ocasio-Cortez’s national profile exploded – bringing in $15m in her first electoral cycle and attracting unprecedented demands from foreign heads of state – Trent tried to lay out a long-term strategic map. He suggested upstate New York events to prepare for a statewide Senate run. But she resisted the logic of political careerism.

“To my chagrin and frustration that never was a way in which she could plan or operate. She did not have an idea in her head of this ultimate prize of president or governor or senator.”

Instead, Trent argues, her appeal lies in a rare authenticity – an ability to validate the deep-seated economic anxiety of Americans. “Alexandria has two things going for her. She’s genuinely curious about other people. It’s not like she has to pretend to be. I’ve had politicians ask me, ‘How can I be more genuine?’ Well, that’s probably not going to help if you have to fucking ask me that.

“Two, she is genuinely open about herself. Some people believe that nobody cares what they think or who they are and then other people don’t want you to know who they are. She doesn’t suffer from either of those failings.”

Other observers agree that Ocasio-Cortez has that X factor missing from so many professional politicians: relatability. Chris Scott, a political strategist who served as the coalition director for Kamala Harris’s 2024 presidential campaign, said: “When you talk about AOC’s humble beginnings being a bartender that’s a lived experience story that resonates, especially with millennials, with their upbringing.

“What you are starting to see – whether it’s conservative or progressive - is people are leaning more and more towards candidates with lived experience that they feel they relate to as politics gets more polarising.”

That said, Ocasio-Cortez has now been in Washington long enough to draw accusations of going from outsider to insider. The activist who critiqued the establishment and championed the Green New Deal has spent recent years working closely with Democratic leadership. This week she received warm praise from Pelosi, who told a Politico summit in Sacramento, California: “I think that she has been so operational, and it’s just wonderful. I know it’s a joy to work with her.”

The transition has caused some on the far left to wonder if the system has simply co-opted its most dangerous critic. Cenk Uygur, a controversial political commentator and co-founder of the online progressive news show The Young Turks, watches Ocasio-Cortez’s recent evolution with a mixture of policy agreement and tactical despair.

Ocasio-Cortez has described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “genocide” and last month voted to block US military aid to the country. But Uygur has not forgotten her high-profile appearance at the 2024 Democratic National Convention, where she delivered a rousing speech praising vice-president Harris’s efforts to secure a ceasefire in Gaza — a claim that many leftwing activists viewed as a dishonest whitewashing of the administration’s complicity in the conflict.

“Why did she basically fib on Kamala Harris’s behalf during the DNC and pretend that Kamala Harris cared about Palestinians and was trying to keep the Israelis in check?” he said. “Because she secretly loves Israel? No, it’s because she wanted to prove to mommy and daddy that she’s a good girl. If you’re a good girl you support Kamala Harris and, if you need to, you fudge her record.

“Then you go tell Jonathan Karl that your side is ‘crazy’ and you changed and you can’t explain what you changed into or how you changed or why you changed. But the message is super clear both for the establishment and progressives: ‘I’m not going to challenge the system so establishment, you can rest easy, I’m not a threat.’ And they have rested easy. That’s why she’s getting enormously positive coverage.”

The 2028 Democratic presidential primary election is expected to be crowded and noisy. If Ocasio-Cortez runs, she might face challenges from fellow progressive Congressman Ro Khanna of California along with heavyweights including Harris, Pete Buttigieg, Gavin Newsom and Jon Ossoff. Some Democrats, scarred by Clinton and Harris’s defeats in 2016 and 2024, might be reluctant to nominate Ocasio-Cortez out of perceived expediency if they believe the US is still not ready to elect its first female president, a fear expressed by former first lady Michelle Obama among others.

The congresswoman faces another potentially formidable hurdle. Centrist Democrats have long argued that the democratic socialist wing of the party might succeed with white, college-educated voters but struggles to connect with African American communities, pointing to primary races where progressive insurgents have hit a wall. That could prove decisive in an early primary state such as South Carolina.

Nina Turner, a national co-chair of Sanders’ 2020 campaign, who has just been travelling in South Carolina, said: “There are some rumblings in some segments of the Black community that DSA and progressives in general are not doing what it takes to court Black voters and in some ways are leaving us behind for other people who are of colour but not Black.

“That’s real and so DSA as well as progressives are going to have to do something to say, no, we understand the Black plight and we understand that the survival of working-class people comes through Black liberation. They have not done a good job of doing that. I’m hoping that they will.”

Antjuan Seawright, a Democratic strategist in South Carolina, suggests that Ocasio-Cortez’s national viability depends on her remaining a disciplined team player who addresses universal, kitchen-table concerns. He said: “I would love her to run as far away as she can from being any sort of liability in places where we know we have to win in November where we’ve lost before because people have been used as a weapon of mass political destruction and distraction.

“If she continues to talk about health care in such a way that is accessible and affordable for all Americans without burning down the system, but making some alterations to the system, she will be a positive voice to the conversation.”

If she runs, Ocasio-Cortez can also expect a crude onslaught from Republicans and a rightwing media machine that has spent years demonising her as a radical communist who threatens the essence of America. Her “Woke One was crazy,” comment has been seen as an attempt to assuage the concern.

Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, said: “That was a very interesting strategic decision to do that and that’s her way of trying to moderate. But she’s palling around with Bernie Sanders and hasn’t completely, as far as I’m aware, repudiated [the influencer] Hasan Piker and some of those leftwing folks. People are not going to forget that and, in this day and age of the internet, it lives forever.”

Setmayer, cofounder of the Seneca Project, a women-led, bipartisan political super political action committee, argues that, instead of campaigning for the White House, Ocasio-Cortez could seek to cement her legislative power by challenging Chuck Schumer for his New York Senate seat.

“If I were advising her, given the failures, unfortunately, of women candidates for the Democrats over the last two election cycles, it would behoove her to run for Senate,” Setmayer said. “She’s almost guaranteed to win that Senate seat.

“It would provide her more gravitas and she’s young enough that she could do a term or two – or a term and a half like Barack Obama – and then run for president. I don’t think that she can go from being a congresswoman to a serious presidential candidate without some time in the Senate.”

History, however, is littered with examples of White House aspirants who waited their turn and missed their moment. There are others, such as Obama, who said “carpe diem” and rode a wave all the way into the Oval Office.

Ocasio-Cortez, who would beat Theodore Roosevelt and John F Kennedy to become the youngest US president in history, has said her ambition is way bigger than that. The calling to change America may prove irresistible.

Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said: “When you look at the current trajectory of the Democratic party, she is the natural successor to the Bernie Sanders-Elizabeth Warren coalition. She is one of the most gifted communicators in all of politics.

“She is someone who engenders a tremendous amount of passion, either for or against. She does possess the unique quality of: people give a shit. She’s got a lot more going for her than most people. She never has to worry about standing out. The attention vacuum that we live in, and the way that content works, she is in a league of her own.”
news.summary:
The New York congresswoman’s power is in the spotlight as people wonder if the stars are finally aligning for her to run for US president in 2028

“They assume that my ambition is positional. They assume that my ambition is a title or a seat. And my ambition is way bigger than that. My ambition is to change this country.”

The words were delivered slowly, deliberately and with some steeliness by Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Her audience, crammed into the pews of Rockefeller Memorial chapel at the University of Chicago, burst into spontaneous applause. That was in May. In the three months since, the speculation around Ocasio-Cortez’s ambitions – for herself and for America – has only grown louder.

news.title: Map Shows Shift in Midterm Districts From 'Solid' Republican to 'Likely'
news.text: Republicans are facing a new potential warning sign heading into the 2026 midterms, with three GOP-held House districts shifting from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican” in the latest ratings from the Cook Political Report. The changes affect two districts in Ohio and one in Colorado, with the report pointing to state-specific political dynamics that could make traditionally favorable territory more competitive for Republicans. Robert Y. Shapiro, professor of political science and in the School of International and Public Affairs at Columbia University, told Newsweek via email on Friday, "This should be of concern to the Republicans and a further wake up call to mobilize their electoral base and voters predisposed against the Democrats." Why It Matters The three shifts highlight how the 2026 midterm environment could put Republican incumbents under pressure even in districts that remain favorable to the GOP. A move from “Solid” to “Likely” Republican does not mean Cook Political expects these seats to become toss-ups. Instead, it signals that the political environment has become less comfortable for Republicans and that state-level races and candidate dynamics could have an impact on House contests. For Republicans, the changes are an early indication that the 2026 map may not be limited to the handful of traditionally competitive battleground districts. If Democrats can capitalize on favorable statewide dynamics in places like Ohio — where Trump won by double digits just two years ago — they could force Republicans to spend resources defending seats that once appeared considerably safer. Midterm elections are commonly seen as a measure of public approval for the current president too, and the president's party has traditionally lost seats during these elections. At present, Republicans maintain a narrow House majority, controlling 218 seats, while Democrats hold 212. With control of the House up for grabs in the upcoming midterm, even modest shifts in the GOP’s favorability could ultimately matter. What To Know Ohio The shift is particularly notable in Ohio, a state that has become increasingly reliable for Republicans in presidential elections. President Donald Trump carried Ohio by roughly 11 percentage points in 2024 versus former Vice President Kamala Harris. Against that backdrop, the Cook Political Report is moving GOP Representative Mike Turner in Ohio’s 10th Congressional District and Mike Carey in the 15th District from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican.” The report says the potential for Democrats to win statewide races, including Sherrod Brown’s Senate bid and Amy Acton’s gubernatorial campaign, could create stronger down-ballot conditions for Democrats. "There’s a decent chance that former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton both carry the 10th District, giving Democrats’ nominee, Kristina Knickerbocker, some coattails to hold on to," Cook Political Report's Erin Covey wrote in part about the 10th District race. "In 2024, Brown lost the district by just one point, and Vivek Ramaswamy’s vulnerabilities with Republican voters have made the governor’s race closer than it should be." Cook Political Report says Ohio’s 15th District remains Republican leaning but could become competitive as Democratic trends strengthen in Columbus’ growing suburbs. Trump won the district by 10 points in 2024, but Senator Bernie Moreno, a Republican, carried it by just 2 points, while Carey won his reelection campaign by 13 points, the report lays out. A July poll commissioned by Democratic-aligned House Majority PAC showed Democrats leading the generic ballot by 3 points, with Carey ahead of Democratic challenger Don Leonard by 5 points, with 45 percent to 40 percent. Carey has a significant financial advantage, with $2 million cash on hand compared with Leonard’s $250,000, the report says and has already reserved $1.5 million in fall advertising. Cook notes that Leonard’s liberal profile makes the race less competitive compared to other Democratic pickup opportunities in the state, while House Majority PAC has reserved another $1.8 million in the race, the report says. Cook Political Report moved Ohio’s 10th District to "Likely" Republican, pointing to signs that the long-held GOP seat could become more competitive. Turner has consistently outperformed the Republican presidential ticket, winning by 18 points in 2024 even as Trump carried the district by 6 percent, but recent polling shows a closer race, the report says. Knickerbocker outraised Turner last quarter, though she ended June with just $125,000, the report says. House Majority PAC has reserved $2.9 million in the district, adding to the potential for a competitive contest. Colorado Colorado presents a different dynamic, but the shift there is also noteworthy. Trump actually lost Colorado by 10 percentage points in 2024, with Harris carrying the state, meaning Colorado itself is not a reliably Republican state. But the 3rd Congressional District represented by Republican Representative Jeff Hurd is more favorable territory for the GOP. Cook Political Report is moving Hurd’s district from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican”, citing recent polling that shows a potentially more competitive race and concerns that the GOP’s gubernatorial nominee, Victor Marx, could hurt Republicans down the ballot. Hurd has an "independent streak," the report notes, that could help him, and the district voted for Trump by 10 points in 2024 and 8 points in 2020. Newsweek reached out to Hurd, Turner and Carey's campaigns via email on Friday for comment. Democratic nominee Dwayne Romero’s campaign released a poll showing Hurd ahead by just one point, 46 percent to 45 percent, though private polling reportedly gives Hurd a larger lead. Hurd also has a major financial advantage, with reportedly $1.8 million available cash compared with Romero’s $84,000, making him better positioned than he was in 2024, the report says. Map Shows Shift in Races from Cook Political What Prediction Markets Show Kalshi shows that Turner has 88 percent compared to Knickerbocker's 14 percent around 11:15 p.m. ET Friday. On Polymarket, the Democratic Party has a 17 percent chance of winning compared to the Republican Party's 83 percent on Friday night. In Ohio's 15th District, Carey has 83 percent on Kalshi on Friday night compared to Leonard's 17 percent. On Polymarket, the Republican Party has 79 percent, and the Democratic Party has a 20 percent chance, Hurd has a 71 percent chance of winning Colorado's 3rd District on Kalshi, compared to Romero's 15 percent. On Polymarket Friday night, the Democratic Party has a 36 percent chance of winning compared to Republicans' 66 percent chance. Election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball says Hurd's race is likely Republican. Shapiro added: "These are ripples of a 'wave election' leading in the direction of the Democrats not only taking control of the House but perhaps having different paths to get a majority in the Senate. In the House, they could get a larger majority than expected. Most important to look for next are incremental shifts in the Senate races that would look better for Democrats in holding on to Senate seats in Michigan and Georgia, and increase their prospects in Maine, North Carolina, Alaska, and Ohio which would be their best shot at four Senate seats to get a majority. But winning Texas offers another route for a bare majority or a more than a 1 seat Senate majority, as would other states that might move away from being solid or leaning Republican and produce a stronger 'wave.'" Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas

news.title: Alaska Democrat Declines Kamala Harris Support Ahead of High-Stakes Senate Primary
news.text:
Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola moved quickly this week to distance herself from former Vice President Kamala Harris, whose 2024 White House bid ended in a double-digit defeat in the state.

In a fundraising appeal, Harris described Alaska as “a must-win Senate seat for Democrats to retake control of the Senate” and asked supporters to “help Mary Peltola get the support she needs” by splitting contributions between Peltola’s campaign and Harris’ Fight for the People PAC.

Harris went on to argue that Peltola is uniquely positioned to make the race competitive, writing, “So if there’s anyone who can flip Alaska and secure the Senate majority for Democrats – it’s Mary. But she cannot do it alone.”

“When we all stand behind Mary, we can give her the boost she needs to overcome their spending and organize across Alaska,” the former vice president added.

Peltola, the former congresswoman who turned Alaska’s at-large House seat blue in 2022, did not embrace the high-profile help from Harris.

“Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 — her focus is and always will be Alaska,” a campaign spokeswoman told the New York Times.

According to the Times, Peltola’s campaign had not signed off on the Harris fundraising email.

Harris lost Alaska to Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election by 14 percentage points.

Republicans quickly moved to link Peltola to Harris after the email went out. 

“Mary Peltola is an ineffective radical leftist who worked hand in hand with Kamala Harris to put Alaska last, so it’s no surprise that Harris is backing Peltola,” National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) spokesman Nick Puglia said in a statement. 

Peltola is one of several candidates challenging incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) in the Aug. 18 nonpartisan Senate primary. 

The top four vote-getters in next week’s contest will advance to the November election. 

Alaskans have not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008.

news.title: Trump thinks AOC is running for president in 2028 and trying to abandon her ‘woke’ policies
news.text:
President Trump claims Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is looking to ditch her “woke” past as part of a 2028 presidential run.

"If you really look at it, they're all saying the same thing," Trump told Fox News on Friday. "They're all trying to disavow themselves from what they said about crime and, well, they're saying, ‘We love sanctuary cities.’"

"I think you're going to see sanctuary cities start to end, because sanctuary cities are a disaster. And somebody like her, she was big for sanctuary cities," Trump added. "They cause crime.”

The president also claimed progressive criminal justice policies such as ending cash bail worsened crime and let killers remain on the street.

Much of the president’s comments were exaggerated or inaccurate.

Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a presidential run, though she recently told The Independent her focus is on more immediate political goals.

“I think my main focus is really genuinely just the midterms right now, and we have to make sure that we win this majority,” she said.

New York’s law ending cash bail applies to misdemeanors and nonviolent crimes, rather than murder.

There is no evidence showing a connection between bail reform and rising crime rates, according to the Brennan Center, and in fact it has been linked to a modest decline in recidivism in New York. 

The New York congresswoman has defended sanctuary cities, however. 

Last year, in a congressional hearing, she described them as a key bulwark against abuse by federal immigration agents, arguing they prevent “attacks on our constitutional rights from illegal search and seizure.”

“There is nothing preventing ICE from issuing a warrant and you having complete compliance,” she said of officials in sanctuary states like New York. 

The president was right about one thing, however; AOC is definitely in the presidential conversation.

In recent days, she’s become the top predicted choice for the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee on prediction sites such as Kalshi and Polymarket. 

Meanwhile, conventional political polls still put former Vice President Kamala Harris at the top spot, with California Governor Gavin Newsom in second and AOC in a distant fourth.

Ocasio-Cortez recently made headlines for detailing the process of freezing her eggs on social media and reflecting on the precarious state of women’s healthcare in America.
