news.title: Trump paints Blakeman as tough on crime with cops as backdrop at New York rally
news.text:
President Donald Trump took his midterm campaign tour to New York's Long Island on Friday, seeking to boost an old friend running for governor and Republicans looking to flip two light-blue House seats.

A native New Yorker, Trump was in Garden City ostensibly, to help Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive who is running to unseat Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul. Trump, who referred to Blakeman as “a friend of mine, for a long time,” made the visit just two days after the release of a Siena University poll that put his unfavorable rating among likely New York voters at 60 percent.

“I'm thrilled to be back in the state I love, and I do love it. So proud of it, but it's going in a bad direction,” Trump said, knocking Hochul without naming her. "We're going to change it around. "We get Bruce in there, we'll change it around.”

The crowd bellowed “Bruuuuuuuce” in unison, garnering a presidential chuckle.

The GOP campaigner in chief said Blakeman’s record on crime was a feather in his gubernatorial campaign cap.

“Under Bruce, think of this: Nassau County has been rated the No. 1 safest county in the United States of America — that's not bad,” Trump said to applause from the uniformed law enforcement personnel seated behind him, many wearing white ceremonial gloves for an occasion that was billed as an official White House event but that mirrored his campaign rallies.

Hochul, though, contended Friday that crime rates were down across the state. Crime data from the state’s Division of Criminal Justice Services showed a 3 percent drop in crimes in New York City between 2024 and 2025 and a 14 percent drop in crimes outside the Big Apple. The crime numbers for both jurisdictions had also declined from 2023.

Blakeman is seen as a decided underdog against Hochul in deep-blue New York, which hasn't elected a Republican governor since 2002. The same Siena poll found Hochul leading Blakeman by 10 points. Forty percent of likely voters didn't know or didn't have an opinion of the Republican nominee, while 33 percent viewed him favorably and 26 percent unfavorably. 

Blakeman appeared onstage for a minute Friday and, like other GOP candidates at Trump events, he praised the headliner: “Thank you, Mr. President, for sealing our borders. … There are less and less … moms and dads that are burying their children from fentanyl, the illegal drugs that came through our porous borders during Biden-Harris. … Keep going.”

In his campaign appearances, Blakeman has reportedly largely refrained from mentioning Trump. But New York Democrats say there is no political daylight between the president and his old friend.

“Bruce Blakeman is Trump’s 100 percent MAGA puppet, mimicking everything from his election denialism, to his healthcare cuts, to his price-hiking agenda,” state Democratic Party spokesperson Addison Dick said in a statement.

New York-based GOP strategist Fay Chapin said Friday that Democrats are attempting to tie all Republicans to the president “because they have nothing else to run on."

“Trump remains an effective turnout tool for Republicans in the suburbs, especially on Long Island. If the attacks are coming anyway, [Blakeman] might as well get the benefits of having the president of the United States come to our neck of the woods,” Chapin said. “I don’t see it backfiring and will only fire up the Republican base in New York, which Blakeman needs in order to win in November.”

Trump greets members of law enforcement as he arrives to deliver remarks Friday in Garden City, N.Y. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images)

Trump’s Empire State campaign stop was his second in three months, following a May 22 event across the Long Island Sound to boost embattled GOP Rep. Mike Lawler in the blue-leaning 17th District. Notably, at that event, Trump mentioned Blakeman and his race more than he did Lawler. 

But Trump’s electoral trend line in Nassau County offers more encouragement for Republicans. After losing the county to Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Joe Biden in 2020, Trump carried it in 2024 over Kamala Harris, becoming the first Republican presidential nominee to win Nassau County since George H.W. Bush in 1988.

More recently, some Empire State voters have been in a different mood, with two establishment-aligned House Democrats from New York City losing to primary challengers backed by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

In total, Mamdani, a self-described democratic socialist who ran on an avowedly progressive platform last year, successfully backed three candidates pushing similar policy ideas during their primary campaigns.

Former New York City Comptroller Brad Lander easily defeated Rep. Dan Goldman in the 10th District Democratic primary. Rep. Adriano Espaillat, chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, lost his primary in the 13th District to community organizer Darializa Avila Chevalier. And a third Mamdani-backed candidate, state Rep. Claire Valdez, defeated Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso in the primary for the 7th District seat being vacated by the retiring Democratic Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez.

Trump has used those victories — and ones by other ultraliberal candidates across the country — to try to paint the entire Democratic Party as being run by communists. Other Republicans have echoed that rhetoric, both in in Washington and on the campaign trail. 

“They continue their war on police and their destruction of the rule of law. The communists want to turn America into a third-world country, into a hellhole of crime and filth,” Trump claimed Friday. “That's why we have to get Bruce into office. … The radical left Gov. Kathy Hochul has been very, very bad on crime."

The GOP messenger in chief is banking that those kinds of arguments will help Republican nominees Mike LiPetri and Jeanine Driscoll in their bids to unseat Democratic Reps. Tom Suozzi in the 3rd District and Laura Gillen in the 4th District respectively. Both districts include sizable portions of Nassau County. Democrats are currently favored in both races, according to Inside Elections with Nathan Gonzales, with the 3rd District rated Lean Democratic and the 4th Tilt Democratic.

LiPetri and Driscoll briefly appeared onstage Friday to deliver a few words to the gathered crowd. Joining them were Republican members of the New York delegation, including Reps. Nicole Malliotakis, Nick LaLota and Andrew Garbarino, who also represents a part of Nassau County. Two other House hopefuls from upstate New York spoke briefly Friday as well: Anthony Constantino, who is running to succeed retiring GOP Rep. Elise Stefanik, and Kailee Buller, who is challenging Democrat John W. Mannion and won an endorsement from Trump on Thursday.

From left, Anthony Constantino, Rep. Andrew Garbarino, Jeanine Driscoll and Trump listen as Mike LiPetri, the GOP nominee for New York's 3rd District, speaks at Friday's event in Garden City. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images)

Trump seemed eager to sway voters by playing up his personal relationship with the GOP gubernatorial nominee — as well as his ability to defy critics. Trump dubbed Blakeman “a great person” and “a friend of mine” and “a great political leader.”

“When Bruce's name came up, I said, ‘Yeah. If they give that guy just a little bit of a chance, just a little bit of fair treatment from the fake news and everyone else, he's going to win,” Trump said. 

But the president also ribbed Blakeman as he pondered being forced to choose between sending his old friend to Albany or New York's Republican congressional delegation back to Washington.

"I don't know, Bruce, I think I'm going to have to give you up," the president quipped. "I want I might have to take the congresspeople."

news.title: Can Gavin Newsom appeal to Nevada voters? Early test for 2028 presidential run
news.text:
As Nevada jockeys to be the second state in the 2028 Democratic presidential nominating calendar, Gov. Gavin Newsom could face an early test of courting voters in a geographic neighbor. After all, Nevada is full of voters who moved across the Sierras to escape California’s stubbornly high cost of living.

For Newsom, the state’s early vote offers possibility and peril. Like California, it’s a diverse state that shares many of the same challenges, from affordability to wildfires. But it is also more politically evenly divided, with a libertarian streak that could be at odds with Newsom’s liberal reputation.

The Democratic National Convention will finalize its early voting calendar at its summer meeting this weekend after the Rules and Bylaws Committee chose South Carolina and Nevada to lead the 2028 primaries, followed by New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.

Newsom, who is believed to be mulling a run for president in 2028, visited the Las Vegas area last month to help the Nevada Democratic Party kick off its canvassing efforts on behalf of U.S. Rep. Steven Horsford and Attorney General Aaron Ford, who is challenging Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. He also flew to Boulder City in March to promote his memoir at the home of Democratic activist Judy Hoskins.

Other prospective 2028 candidates like Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Obama White House official Rahm Emanuel, and Arizona U.S. Sen. Ruben Gallego have also visited the state in recent months. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg will appear Saturday at a Reno-area Democratic fundraiser.

Steve Sisolak, who served as the state’s last Democratic governor from 2019 to 2023, said Newsom was held in “very high regard” among members of his party.

“He’s highly liked and well regarded,” Sisolak said, calling Newsom “very approachable” and “exceptionally helpful” when it came to solving shared issues like wildfires, the shrinking Colorado River, and interstate highway traffic.

Still, Sisolak pointed out that Nevada Democrats tended to downplay their support for Newsom, pointing to a Republican campaign billboard highlighting Newsom’s support of Ford (“Gavin Newsom endorses Aaron Ford”) as a negative. Lombardo also derided Newsom’s “tax-and-spend” agenda in response to a recent Las Vegas Review-Journal op-ed.

“The idea is that Newsom’s support would detract from Aaron Ford,” Sisolak said, as Republicans have hit the California governor for his state’s high housing costs and homelessness crisis.

California has lost 900,000 people since 2015 to other states, including over 300,000 to Nevada since 2018, according to reports from the Public Policy Institute of California and Nevada Real Estate Group. The think tank found that the top reason people cited for moving was high housing costs, followed by jobs and family reasons.

Newsom’s office has pushed back on reports of population loss as a right-wing media narrative, calling it “California Derangement Syndrome.”

A recent Emerson College poll found Newsom led the field of 12 prospective 2028 contenders at 37% support among Nevada Democrats, followed by Buttigieg, 19%; New York U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 9%; and former Vice President Kamala Harris, 6%.

A source in Newsom’s orbit who declined to be identified to preserve their relationship with the governor also noted the same poll showed Ford and Lombardo in a dead heat ahead of the November general election.

“There’s a reason Aaron Ford was comfortable campaigning with Newsom: he’s popular with Democratic voters in the state,” the Newsom ally said.

Sisolak said Nevada would be an important state for any Democrat to win, citing its high union density, particularly the influential Culinary Workers union, and its diverse populations of Latinos and swiftly growing Asian American and Pacific Islander and Black communities.

“It touches all of the demographics you want to reach,” he said. “You can test your message, see how it resonates, and get off to a good start, then focus (in other states).”

A strategist close to the Nevada Democratic Party who spoke anonymously because they were not authorized to speak to the media said national candidates need to adopt a “ground game” strategy early as the 2028 primary season starts up.

“We’re not an Iowa or a New Hampshire where you can go in and stand up a team on a Tuesday, and hit voters,” the strategist said. “Elections here are won by a field organizing margin. That means you need to go to a casino, and talk to workers there, or go to a construction site and talk to people there. Having a presence goes a long way here.”

Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders handily won the state in the 2020 Democratic primary, which national media attributed to support from a multiracial coalition of young liberal voters who were drawn to his economic populist message.

The Democratic strategist called Sanders’ victory an “apple-to-oranges” comparison, as Nevada was still an early caucus state then, whereas it will host its first competitive early presidential primary in 2028. Caucus states are when local parties choose their candidates, while in primaries voters elect the candidate of their choosing.

The strategist pointed towards a recent Third Way survey that found most Democratic Nevada primary voters favored candidates who could speak to a broad swath of voters over progressive ideals, which they said reflected the state’s libertarian streak.

“We want to be able to carry our guns, but we also want to be able to access abortion,” they said. “Ultimately, (a candidate’s ability to win) comes down to their ability to talk about how they’re able to stand up for Nevada and issues Nevadans care about, not about working with one party over another. It’s about working across the aisle and finding solutions, not party ideals.”

Erik Jimenez, the chair of the Washoe County Democrats, said affordability was a major concern as high wage-earning Californians have moved east. Lured by remote work and employers like Tesla and Amazon to the Reno area, the transplants contributed to that area’s housing shortage, which is now among the worst in the U.S.

“It’s a tough challenge to solve,” Jimenez said. “We’re super open to ‘how can we continue to grow’ but in northern Nevada, 90% of the land is owned by the federal government. There are limited resources to do new things. We can’t necessarily just build up new housing stock.”

Both he and the Democratic strategist both said Newsom would need to craft an economic message that could resonate with Nevada voters, while downplaying the idea that Republicans’ linking Newsom with California’s ongoing affordability crisis would sink his chances as someone who is frequently viewed as progressive in other parts of the country.

“Nevada Republicans consistently push the concept of ‘don’t California my Nevada,’ this idea that Democrats want these seemingly liberal California policies,” the strategist said. “We’ve seen that fail to resonate or move the needle in elections.”

Jimenez pointed out that northern Nevada still remains a competitive part of the state, and that the Democratic Party there welcomes a wide coalition of leftists to moderates. He said Nevada progressives seemed to be emboldened by recent wins in states like New York and Michigan over moderate incumbents.

“We are seeing the youth of the party going more towards what’s going on in Michigan, and pushing us to be more progressive in our thinking,” he said.

He also anticipated Newsom and other candidates will need to address data centers, which Nevada was an early investor in, and which now have become the target of bipartisan backlash.

“We have acute resource concerns about that, in a way that you won’t see in South Carolina,” Jimenez said.

news.title: Fox News Polls Show Democrats Chances of Beating GOP to Flip Senate: Map
news.text: Democrats are increasingly competitive in their bid to reclaim control of the Senate in the November midterm elections, according to a series of recent Fox News polls showing the party's nominees narrowly ahead in several key battlegrounds that would be critical to securing a majority. While Republicans are ahead in Michigan, a Democratic-held seat, Fox News polls show Democratic candidates leading in six other battleground seats: Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Texas and Maine. Those gains would be enough to overcome a loss in Michigan and still deliver a Democratic majority if the party has a net gain of four seats on November 3. Strategists caution, however, that several of those states have leaned Republican in recent federal and state elections and that polls are not indicators of election results. Still, the overall Senate landscape remains challenging for Democrats, and more recent polling in several key races has painted a more favorable picture for Republicans, who enter the cycle with a 53-47 majority. Many of the states where Democrats currently hold leads have voted Republican in recent presidential elections, but Democrats believe that President Donald Trump's slipping approval rating and ongoing war with Iran, among other policy priorities, could help their campaigns. Although Fox News is often seen as favoring Republican viewpoints, its polling arm is generally well regarded by political observers across the spectrum and has ranked among the nation's more accurate pollsters. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat, is taking on Republican Mike Collins in one of the most closely watched races this cycle. Ossoff was elected in January 2021, defeating Republican incumbent David Perdue in a closely watched runoff election. His victory, along with that of fellow Democrat Raphael Warnock, marked a historic shift in Georgia’s political landscape, long considered a Republican stronghold. Collins has represented Georgia's 10th Congressional District in the House since 2023. Trump endorsed him in the primary run-off on June 16, writing in part, in a Truth Social post: “Mike is strongly supported by the most Highly Respected MAGA Patriots in Georgia and beyond, and many Republicans in the U.S. House and Senate — He is a WARRIOR and WINNER!” Georgia has become a battleground in recent election cycles. Trump carried the state by about 2 percentage points in 2024 after Joe Biden narrowly won it in 2020, marking the first Democratic presidential victory there since 1992. Republicans continue to hold the governor's office, while Democrats hold both U.S. Senate seats, highlighting the state's competitive political landscape. A June 23-27 Fox News poll surveyed 1,002 Georgia registered voters, finding Ossoff in the lead with 56 percent support to Collins' 43 percent. The poll found Ossoff with a 58 percent favorability rating and Collins with 44 percent, both ahead of Trump's 42 percent. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The University of Virginia's Center for Politics shifted Georgia's Senate race from “lean Democratic” to “likely Democratic” in its latest Crystal Ball ratings last month. Recent public polling has generally shown Ossoff with a mid-to-high single-digit lead. Newsweek has reached out to the Ossoff and Collins campaigns for comment via email on Friday. North Carolina The North Carolina Senate race between Democratic former Governor Roy Cooper and Republican Michael Whatley is expected to be one of the most competitive of the midterms, with Democrats viewing it as one of their top flip opportunities. The state has frequently produced ticket-splitting outcomes, with voters supporting candidates from both parties in statewide and federal contests. North Carolina is an electoral battleground that backed Trump by about 3 points in 2024. Two-term Republican Senator Thom Tillis announced he was retiring at the end of his term, leaving vacant—and vulnerable—a battleground seat. Democrats believe Cooper, a two-term governor, is a strong candidate who can flip the seat in a favorable national environment, fueled by Trump’s declining national approval rating. Republicans, however, note that most polling still shows Cooper below 50 percent support and that the state has favored their candidates in recent federal elections. A July Fox News poll of 1,005 North Carolina registered voters found Cooper with a 9-point lead, 53 percent to Whatley’s 44 percent, with about 2 percent undecided. The poll found Cooper with a 54 percent favorability rating and Whatley and Trump both at 40 percent. The poll was conducted July 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as a “Lean Democrat.” Other recent polling has shown Cooper, who benefits from high name recognition, with a lead. A New York Times and Siena poll, which surveyed 601 likely voters June 15-27, showed Cooper with a 7-point lead at 50 percent support to Whatley’s 43 percent. Newsweek has reached out to the Cooper and Whatley campaigns for comment via email on Friday. Ohio Republican Senator Jon Husted is facing off former Senator Sherrod Brown in Ohio. Brown, who lost his reelection bid in 2024, is seeking a comeback in a special election against Husted, who was appointed by Governor Mike DeWine to fill the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance. Trump carried the state by about 11 percentage points in 2024, an improvement on his 2020 and 2016 performances, when he won by about 8 points in each. But Ohio was viewed as more competitive for Democrats not long before. President Barack Obama narrowly carried Ohio in 2008 and 2012. It has shifted as Trump performed well among the state’s working-class voters. Ohio has been competitive in some recent elections. Brown won reelection in 2018, then lost in 2024 by fewer than 4 percentage points. Democrats hope their candidates can improve on that this year in a more favorable national environment. An August Fox News poll found Brown leading Husted by 8 points, 53 percent to 45 percent, with about 2 percent undecided. Brown leads among independents in Ohio by 38 points, 66 percent to 28 percent for Husted. The poll of 1,008 registered Ohio voters was conducted August 6-10. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball view the race as a pure toss-up. Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted it from Lean Republican earlier in June after Brown and Husted formally won their parties’ nominations. Husted campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce told Newsweek in an email Friday: “Sherrod Brown spent 32 years in Washington raising Ohioans' taxes and giving benefits to illegal immigrants. Polls will go up and down all summer. What won’t change is that voters fired Brown two years ago after looking at his record of failure, and they’re not willing to go backwards now." Newsweek has reached out to Brown’s campaign for comment via email on Friday. Iowa Republican Representative Ashley Hinson is going against Democratic state Representative Josh Turek in the Iowa Senate race. They are running to succeed Republican Senator Joni Ernst, who chose not to run for reelection. Democrats haven't secured a Senate seat in the state since Tom Harkin's election in 2008. Turek is a two-time Paralympic gold medalist and state House member, first elected in 2022. Obama endorsed him in a late-July video, while Trump has endorsed Hinson, who was first elected in 2020 after serving in the state House and working as a journalist. Iowa was viewed as a battleground for much of the 2000s, with Obama carrying the state by about 10 points in 2008 and 6 points in 2012. But Trump performed well in the state in each of his presidential bids, winning by 10 points in 2016, 8 points in 2020 and 13 points in 2024. A Fox News poll of 1,003 Iowa registered voters found Turek leading Hinson 50 percent to 46 percent, with 4 percent undecided. The poll was conducted June 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. An Emerson poll this month found Hinson with a slight lead, 47.5 percent to 45 percent. She was viewed favorably by 44 percent of respondents and unfavorably by 40 percent, while Turek was viewed favorably by 42 percent and unfavorably by 27 percent. It surveyed 712 likely voters August 2-4 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as “leans Republican.” Polling averages suggest a competitive contest. RealClearPolling's average shows the race nearly tied, with Hinson having 47 percent support and Turek 46.3 percent. Newsweek has reached out to the Turek and Hinson campaigns for comment via email on Friday. Texas The GOP's decadeslong hold on Texas statewide offices will be tested in November, with the Senate race between Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Representative James Talarico nearly deadlocked. Texas has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, making it one of the nation's longest-running Republican strongholds. Democrats have repeatedly targeted the state as demographic shifts and population growth have reshaped its electorate, but they have fallen short in a series of closely watched campaigns, including Beto O'Rourke's 2018 Senate bid against Ted Cruz. Surveys show both Paxton, who is endorsed by Trump, and Talarico, who has served as a state representative since 2018, holding narrow leads at different points in the campaign. The matchup comes after Paxton defeated longtime Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary in late May. A Fox News poll of 1,006 registered Texas voters found that 51 percent back Talarico and 48 percent Paxton, with 1 percent undecided. The survey was conducted July 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. However, polls appear to flip-flop on who is leading, as a recent Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters puts the Senate race in a near dead heat, with 47 percent backing Paxton and 46 supporting Talarico. About 5 percent are undecided and 2 percent back a different candidate. The poll was conducted August 9-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as “leans Republican.” Newsweek has reached out to the Talarico and Paxton campaigns for comment via email on Friday. Maine In Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins faces a competitive reelection bid from Democrat Troy Jackson, who became his party's nominee after Graham Platner withdrew from the race. Platner, who won the primary in June, formally withdrew from the race after allegations emerged about his past conduct, including accusations of inappropriate behavior and alleged sexual assault, which he has denied. A Fox News poll conducted August 6-10 found Jackson ahead of Collins 48 percent to 46 percent, putting the race within the poll's 3 percent margin of error, highlighting how close the election could be. According to the poll, which surveyed 1,000 registered voters in the state, Jackson’s strongest support comes from liberals, younger voters, college-degree holders and union households. He also leads among voters under 45, while men overall are evenly split between the two candidates. Collins’ support is strongest among conservatives, white evangelical Christians, voters without college degrees, and rural voters, the poll shows. A Fox News poll in June showed Collins with 50 percent to Platner's 47 percent. Both Sabato’s Crystal Ball and The Cook Political Report categorize Maine as a toss-up. Newsweek has reached out to the Jackson and Collins campaigns for comment via email on Friday. Michigan With Democrats eyeing a Senate comeback, Michigan is widely viewed as a must-win battleground. The state backed Trump in two of the past three presidential elections, but Democrats have continued to notch major statewide victories, emphasizing Michigan's status as one of the nation's most closely divided battlegrounds. Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed will go against Republican Mike Collins for the open Senate seat following Democrat Gary Peters' decision to retire. Democrats have held the seat for decades. In 2016, Democratic primary voters backed independent Vermont Senator Sanders over Hillary Clinton before narrowly helping deliver the state to Trump months later. news.title: Kristen Stewart Considers Moving to Europe if Midterm Elections ‘Start a Civil War’: ‘It’s a Privilege’
news.text:
Kristen Stewart may be the next A-lister to move out of the U.S. for political reasons.
“If the midterms don’t start a Civil War, that’d be cool. I dream this,” Stewart, 36, told Owen Thiele on the Thursday, August 13, episode of the “In Your Dreams” podcast. “I don’t want to leave. I like it here. But I will [leave].”
Stewart was discussing her current “big dream” with Thiele, 29, and her The Wrong Girls costar Alia Shawkat on the podcast when the host asked whether she was seriously considering moving to Europe depending on the results of November’s midterm elections.
“It’s a privileged thing to say but even on a smaller scale, an escape hatch is totally f***ing necessary,” Stewart replied.
The Twilight actress has a notorious history with President Donald Trump, as the politician routinely insulted her during her past relationship with ex-boyfriend Robert Pattinson.
Four years before his 2016 presidential campaign, Trump, 80, tweeted that Stewart “cheated on [Pattinson] like a dog” and urged the actor to dump her. (At the time, Stewart had publicly apologized to then-boyfriend Pattinson, 40, for having a fling with her Snow White and the Huntsman director, Rupert Sanders.)
“[Trump] was mad at me a couple years ago, really obsessed with me a couple years ago, which is f***ing crazy,” Stewart later told Variety in 2016. “I can’t even understand it. I literally cannot even understand it. It’s such a far-out concept that I don’t want to believe that actually is happening. It’s insane.”
Stewart would be far from the first celebrity to move out of the U.S. over political disagreements with the Trump administration.
Ellen DeGeneres confirmed during a July 2025 interview that she and wife Portia de Rossi chose to make a “part-time” move to the U.K. permanent after Trump beat former Vice President Kamala Harris in the November 2024 presidential election.
“We got here the day before the election and woke up to lots of texts from our friends with crying emojis, and I was like, 'He got in'," DeGeneres, 68, recalled. "And we're like, 'We're staying here'."
Rosie O’Donnell moved to Ireland in January 2025 on the eve of her longtime nemesis Trump’s second inauguration amid his threats to revoke her citizenship. (O’Donnell has since returned to the U.S. on a temporary basis for her one-woman Off-Broadway show Common Knowledge.)
“I know myself enough to know that this was something I needed to do for the safety and sanity of myself and my non-binary child,” O’Donnell, 64, exclusively told Us in April 2025.
The midterm elections will be held on November 3 to determine which major party controls the House of Representatives and the Senate in 2027.

news.title: Please, Karl Rove, Stop Trying to Help
news.text:
Karl Rove has another seven-step plan for Republicans. Apparently, the GOP's biggest problem in 2026 is a shortage of advice from Karl Rove.

Political commentator Rove served as senior adviser and deputy chief of staff to President George W. Bush. His latest prescription says President Donald Trump missed the mark in Las Vegas.

Republicans should stop telling voters everything is wonderful, quit leaning so heavily on the word "communist," use Democrats' own words against them, force candidates to defend old positions and radical allies, and offer more concrete policies in 2027. From Rove's website:

The victories of far-left Senate Democratic candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Troy Jackson in Maine, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota and others in assorted House districts give Republicans openings for the midterms, but only if handled correctly.President Trump missed the mark last week in Las Vegas when promoting his tax exclusion for tips. He opened the argument smartly, saying Republicans are “working every day to defend the American Dream for you and your children.”But then he claimed “the radical left, the maniacs, they’re trying to destroy it with the disaster known as not socialism [but] communism. . . . These are communists.” Mr. Trump suggested Republicans should say that if Democrats prevail, then “you’ll have nothing but death, squalor, poverty.”This might have cheered his true believers but didn’t gain a single vote. Instead, it showed that he doesn’t understand public opinion, how he got elected, or what it’ll take to win this fall.In the RealClearPolitics average of recent polls, Mr. Trump’s overall approval rating is 39%. On specific issues, his numbers are often worse. On handling inflation, it’s 31%; Iran, 36%; Russia and Ukraine, 37%; the economy, 37%; foreign policy, 38%. He exceeds his overall approval number only on immigration (44%) and crime (45%). Even then, a majority disapprove of his handling of every issue.The president dismisses bad numbers as “fake polls.” But his pollsters probably see similar results.

Some of Rove's advice is perfectly sensible; voters know what groceries, rent, and gasoline cost because they pay the bills. Republicans shouldn't insult them by pretending every economic concern has vanished.

He's also right that Democrats' own words are often more damaging than anything a Republican consultant could invent.

Then Rove cites Trump's devastating 2024 "they/them" ad against Kamala Harris as the model Republicans should follow.

In other words, one of his best ideas is to do what Trump already figured out. A year ago.

Rove also isn't really asking Republicans to stop attacking socialists. He wants them to stop shouting "communist" and expecting the label to persuade swing voters.

Fair enough; if that's the grand revelation, Republicans can probably survive without another seminar.

The Democratic Socialists of America already supplies enough material. Its current program imagines a future where people don't pay mortgages or have landlords. It calls for publicly owned social housing and universal rent control. On crime, it advocates steps toward "fully abolishing the police and prison system."

Republicans don't need to improve those words. Read them aloud.

Ask Democrat candidates whether they agree. Ask whether homeownership should remain a primary way working families build wealth. Ask what replaces police and prisons. 

Make every Democrat sharing a ballot with DSA-backed candidates answer those questions.

Rove deserves credit for recognizing the opportunity. He loses me when he packages common sense as another consultant's master plan while scolding Trump for supposedly failing to understand how he got elected. From Rove's website:

No longer. But these reluctant 2024 Trump supporters are still crucial. Winning them over this fall requires that Republicans do seven things.First, don’t gaslight voters. The president claimed in Las Vegas that he produced “the greatest economy we’ve ever had so far” with “the cost of rent, groceries and other staples . . . coming down very fast.” How many swing voters believe that? Claims that collide with Americans’ day-to-day experience got Mr. Biden into trouble and now Mr. Trump, too.Second, screaming “communist” won’t win additional votes. Instead, use a Democratic candidate’s own words and policies. Remember the Trump 2024 “they/them” ad, featuring footage of Kamala Harris endorsing transgender surgery for convicts? Make Democratic candidates eat anything they say that’s extreme.Third, don’t let Democrats get away with disavowing past outrageous positions. Point out how convenient their changes are. Ask when and why they changed their minds. Raise doubts, suggesting that they’re untrustworthy and nothing keeps them from reverting to those extreme views.Fourth, don’t let Democrats escape from dangerous associations. If someone like Hasan Piker campaigned for them or another Democrat on the state ticket, make every Democrat defend every terrible comment Mr. Piker has made. Ask why Democrats would ever associate with someone like that.Fifth, Republicans—especially those running against candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America or opponents who share their state ticket with DSA-backed Democrats—must explain why the DSA’s agenda won’t work and will hurt voters. The DSA doesn’t want Americans to have a landlord or mortgage. That logically means the government would assign your housing and you couldn’t accumulate wealth by buying a home and letting it grow in value.Sixth, force normal Democrats to disavow DSA policies. Yes, that gives some Democrats an opportunity to say they won’t abolish ICE, defund the police or close prisons. But that could discourage some of their left-wing supporters from turning out.

Trump won the presidency twice, and maybe Rove might consider allowing for the possibility that Trump understands his coalition.

Rove's final complaint has more merit. President Trump spent little time in Las Vegas explaining his healthcare proposal or the SAVE America Act. Republican candidates need specific plans for what comes next. Voters deserve reasons to support Republicans beyond reasons to oppose Democrats. From the Associated Press:

Retired boxing champ Mike Tyson made an appearance at Trump’s speech, sitting with Rick Harrison of television show “Pawn Stars” and Gov. Joe Lombardo.Trump gave a shout out to Tyson from the stage, saying he saw his Broadway show called “Mike Tyson: Undisputed Truth.”“I’ve seen a lot of Broadway shows, and he was fantastic,” Trump said.Trump revives little-mentioned health care planThe president toward the end of his remarks in Las Vegas said that with the help of a Republican-controlled Congress, “We will pass the Great Healthcare Plan. It’s called the Great Healthcare Plan.”Trump announced the outlines of the plan in January, but he has spent little time speaking about it since then.The centerpiece of his proposal is to send money directly to Americans for health savings accounts to pay for insurance and health costs.Trump says ‘we may have to’ send oil prices higherAs he often does, the president predicted that oil prices will fall once the war in Iran is over – something he has been saying for weeks, but which has yet to fully come to fruition.Trump, however, added a new wrinkle in his Las Vegas speech. He noted that the price of oil has stabilized somewhat recently, “And we may have to send it up again.”“We may have to — you know what happens when we send it up. But we hope we don’t have to,” the president said.He didn’t clarify what he meant by that. But oil prices have typically risen as the war in Iran continues — despite Trump’s repeated assurances that the conflict will soon be over.

Rove helped W. win two presidential elections. Credit where it's due.

However, the Republican Party has changed, its voters have changed, and its political language has changed. The Wing-T offense was an effective football strategy until the defenses adapted. Karl, enjoy the columns, television appearances, and memories.

Please stop trying to help.

news.title: What we know about the alleged Iranian hacks on US water utilities
news.text:
Since the end of last month, several water utilities in the United States have been hit by cyberattacks, causing alarm in the country. 

For years, water utilities and other critical infrastructure facilities in the power sector, for example, have been targeted by hackers, whether government-backed or individuals. What makes this recent series of attacks—allegedly carried out by Iran—particularly concerning was how widespread they have been, hitting targets in around a dozen states. 

The U.S. has more than 150,000 water systems, some of them run by local companies. In theory, that should make it harder for hackers to target several facilities at the same time. But on the flip side, the companies running these systems may not have the resources or cybersecurity expertise needed to protect themselves. 

Cybersecurity experts have long believed that Iranian hackers target low-hanging fruit in opportunistic isolated attacks, so this hacking campaign could be a significant escalation. 

A lot has happened since news of the initial attacks broke two weeks ago. So we decided it was a good time to recap what we know so far, and what we don’t. 

Where have there been attacks?

On July 28, Minnesota authorities announced that water treatment plants in more than 30 communities were hit by coordinated cyberattacks. 

Two days later, the FBI said water and wastewater utility companies in “at least seven states” reported incidents, and in some cases the attacks “degraded water operations.” Since then, apart from Minnesota, there have been reported hacks against water facilities in Arkansas, Georgia, New Jersey, and Michigan. 

Who is behind the attacks?

The short answer is: we don’t know yet, but the number one suspect is the Iranian government. 

As of today, officially, the U.S. government has yet to name the culprit behind the coordinated wave of hacks.

However, the first incidents in Minnesota came days after the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned that Iranian hackers were targeting internet-connected devices in water systems and the energy sector, without saying where those attacks were occurring. (CISA had originally published this warning in April, and updated it before the Minnesota attacks.) 

After the initial wave was uncovered in Minnesota, President Donald Trump said he did not think “there was an Iranian cyberattack.” Instead, he blamed the state, perhaps because it is run by democratic governor Tim Walz, who was chosen as Kamala Harris’s vice president in the 2024 elections.

Trump’s claim came a day after Wired reported that the Water Information Sharing and Analysis Center, or WaterISAC, a nonprofit group that distributes cybersecurity information among the water sector, told its members that the recent attacks “aligned” with the hacking campaign CISA warned of—effectively accusing the Iranian government. 

Earlier this week, The Washington Post reported that U.S. intelligence agencies “are confident” that Iran, and in particular the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), is responsible. The attribution isn’t public yet, according to the paper’s sources, because the agencies are not sure which specific unit within the IRGC was responsible, and also because officials may be reluctant to contradict Trump’s claim.

Iranian government hackers have a history of targeting critical infrastructure in the U.S., and it’s possible that these attacks are part of its strategy to retaliate against the country because of the six-month-long war. 

Until now, Iranian hackers had had only limited success in their cyberattacks against U.S. targets. In March, a hacktivist group called Handala disrupted the operations of medical tech giant Stryker. The U.S. government later accused Handala of being operated by Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). Then, the group claimed responsibility for hacking the personal Gmail account of FBI director Kash Patel.

What effects have the attacks had?

The reality is that some systems inside critical infrastructure facilities are exposed to the internet and relatively easy to find. Earlier this month, cybersecurity firm Forescout reported finding more than 2,800 controllers in U.S. water systems exposed online. If a system is exposed, it doesn’t automatically mean hackers can take over control and cause real-world effects. But that has happened in some isolated cases in recent attacks.

The FBI said some of the cyberattacks around the country caused loss of pressure, which “could potentially allow untreated groundwater to seep into pipes,” and flooding. 

The town of Braham in Minnesota, one of the first ones to report an incident, had to take its water plant offline for a few hours, urging its around 1,700 residents to conserve water. The city of Maple Plain, also in Minnesota, briefly declared a state of emergency. In a county outside Atlanta, Georgia, local officials briefly told residents to boil water before using it as a precautionary measure. 

The worst effect, however, may be psychological. These attacks have been widely covered in national and local press, causing people to worry about the safety of a fundamental and basic need like water. That may very well be part of the hackers’ goals: to spread panic and fear.
news.summary: Over the last couple of weeks, hackers have targeted and broken into the systems of several water plants in the United States. Here’s what we know and don’t know about this wave of attacks allegedly carried out by the Iranian government.

news.title: Trump Cabinet member’s video reveals her office is festooned with pictures of herself
news.text:

This is the August 14, 2026, edition of “The Tea, Spilled by Morning Joe” newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered straight to your inbox every Monday through Friday.

It’s been nine months. 

Nine months since the USS Abraham Lincoln pulled out of San Diego in what was supposed to be a routine seven-month cruise.

And here they still sit — 5,000 sailors and Marines, hundreds of days at sea. A record no crew should have to break. 

From my years on the Armed Services Committee, I know that breaking such records also breaks down the morale of American servicemen and -women. 

Twice, Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon promised those servicemen and -women, “You’re almost home.” 

And twice, that promise was broken.

Military readiness is not limited to the state of advanced weapon systems. It’s also affected by sailors and Marines being forced to sleep in moldy rooms, drink contaminated water, work with no time off, and remain separated from their children, spouses, parents, and loved ones longer than any military leader should ever consider acceptable. 

Hegseth’s cartoonish celebration of war, his advocacy of endless conflicts and invasions, and his continued failure to plan ahead — whether for munition supplies or troop deployments — has left the Navy with too few carriers to relieve those who need it most. 

So the most exhausted ship crew continues its mission in an all-too-avoidable war.

While Hegseth dithers, American readiness bleeds — and that undermines the next crisis, the next conflict, and the next war he will beg to start. 

Meanwhile, the Lincoln’s battered crew continues standing watch, doing the job asked of it, and defending its country. Even if the secretary of defense they ultimately answer to is not.

ON THE CALENDAR

In Boston, the David Chesnut Jazz Festival is back for its fourth year at the Eustis Estate on Saturday. Chesnutwas a coachman there in the 1890s who lived for music. Jazz on the lawn, all afternoon. He’d have liked that.

In New York, this is your last weekend to catch Greater New York 2026 at MoMA PS1. Fifty artists fill every floor of the old schoolhouse, exploring the city in all its layered, lived-in texture. If you’ve been meaning to go, the clock is ticking. 

In the nation’s capital, pandas — the vibe, the merch, the dumplings — are taking over Pennsylvania Avenue. Panda Fest is an outdoor Asian food festival packed with sushi, panda-shaped treats, and a general atmosphere of joyful excess.

news.title: How Kamala Harris accidentally sold the SAVE America Act
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2028 presidential front-runner, recently criticized the SAVE America Act because it would require people to prove their citizenship when registering to vote.

Sometimes the strongest argument for legislation comes from the people trying to defeat it.

Requiring someone to establish that he is a U.S. citizen before being added to the voter rolls is not some hidden provision critics just uncovered. It is the point of the bill.

The SAVE America Act would require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship before registration for federal elections. Harris meant that as an indictment. Supporters see it as the safeguard at the heart of the legislation.

Recent events are making the distinction harder to dismiss.

Last month, the Department of Homeland Security warned election officials in California, New Jersey, Nevada, and Pennsylvania that tens of thousands of noncitizens appeared on state voter rolls.

Less than a week later, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill (D) acknowledged that roughly 6,600 noncitizens had been registered because of what she called a “software glitch.”

Calling it a software glitch may explain how it happened. It does not answer the more important question: Why did the system allow it to happen at all?

New Jersey does not prove that every state has the same problem, and an erroneous registration is not the same thing as an illegal vote. But it does demonstrate the basic case for prevention rather than cleanup.

How long did the vulnerability exist? Why was it not caught sooner? And why should states wait until ineligible registrations occur before verifying eligibility?

The New Jersey episode becomes even more revealing because lawmakers had already spotted the weakness.

In May, state Sens. Jim Beach (D) and Kristin Corrado (R) introduced bipartisan legislation intended to prevent New Jersey's Motor Vehicle Commission from prompting people to register to vote after they had already indicated they were not U.S. citizens.

Think about that for a second.

The software glitch did not invent the vulnerability. It exposed a problem legislators were already trying to fix. That is precisely why supporters of the SAVE America Act want safeguards at the front end of registration, before election officials are left explaining how ineligible names reached the rolls.

As Texas Public Policy Foundation Chief National Initiatives Officer Chuck DeVore wrote in “How to Ensure That Only Citizens Vote,” “When non-citizens vote for any reason, citizens’ votes are diluted and thus disenfranchised.”

RELATED: The SAVE America Act cannot save this electorate

 Bill Pugliano/Getty Images

The argument is not that eligible Americans should face needless obstacles. It is that citizenship should be established before someone is placed on a federal voter roll, protecting the weight of every lawful ballot.

That position is hardly outside the mainstream.

A recent Fox News poll found that 83% of registered voters favored requiring photo identification to register and 77% favored requiring it to cast a ballot.

Most Americans appear to regard verification as a reasonable expectation, not an extraordinary burden. Which makes the Democrats' position even stranger.

Earlier this year, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said Democrats support voter ID.

Then came the vote. Senate Democrats opposed Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted's voter ID bill, which would have required voters to present valid identification before receiving a ballot in federal elections.

So what exactly do they support?

The debate has become almost comically inverted. Critics say proof of citizenship goes too far. Democrat leaders say they support voter ID. Then, when a voter ID requirement reaches the Senate floor, they vote against it.

Meanwhile, New Jersey has supplied a real-world example of what happens when verification comes too late.

Kamala Harris meant to make the case against the SAVE America Act. Instead, she described exactly why its supporters want it.

The contradiction now extends well beyond Harris: Democrats say they support verification while opposing the mechanisms designed to perform it.

Sometimes the strongest argument for legislation comes from the people trying to defeat it.

AOC hasn’t confirmed that she is running yet, of course, though her non-denials have become considerably less coy. ‘I haven’t ruled out the possibility,’ she told ABC last week. ‘And I’m very humbled by the tremendous amount of support out there.’

The arguments against AOC 2028 are well-rehearsed. A dues-paying member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), she’s way too far to the left of America’s mainstream. She’s a goofy millennial feminist, riddled with internet-induced narcissism, who overshares and annoys people. This week, for instance, she began a series of selfie-videos ‘documenting’ her egg-freezing process for her 9.7 million followers on Instagram. To most decent people, that’s extremely cringe-inducing.

She’s never been a senator or a governor. And for all her self-confidence and proficiency in issuing progressive soundbites, she can sound foolish – especially when discussing foreign policy. In February, she attended the Munich Security Conference, and was widely mocked for her ‘word salads’ as she participated in various panels. She fumbled a response about the future of Taiwan, and said that Venezuela was south of the equator when it is not. ‘She had no idea what was happening,’ remarked President Trump, gleefully.

But sounding stupid on the world stage never dented Kamala Harris’s ambition, and she too is understood to be preparing another tilt at the presidency in 2028. In fact, AOC’s real opportunity might boil down to the fact that her likely primary opponents are older and even more flawed than she is. Gavin Newsom, the oily and disaster-prone Governor of California, is now the second favourite behind her to the Democratic nominee.

What AOC has in her favour is what modern politicians crave most of all – a brand. She has international name-recognition and tens of millions of followers across social media. And, at a time when Americans are sick of living under an incompetent gerontocracy, her youth is highly appealing.

For many young left-liberals, her online phoniness is in fact an indication of authenticity. She’s still good-looking, too, which is a powerful asset in our hyper-visual age. She is capable, moreover, of shrewdly positioning herself as a sort of bridge between the populist radical left of the Democratic party, with all its organisational muscle, and the more broadly palatable centre.

Though she utters all the correct progressive pieties about the ‘genocide in Gaza,’ Wall Street greed and ‘healthcare for all,’ AOC has been careful to eschew some of the extreme rhetoric of her fellow DSA members. Indeed, in 2024, the DSA withdrew its endorsement of her after she declined to oppose funding for Israel’s Iron Dome, voted in favour of Israel’s right to exist and hosted a panel on anti-Semitism.

She now insists she does oppose US military aid for Israel – though she still does not go far enough in her criticisms of the Jewish state for the more rabid fringes of her movement. This more nuanced position makes her more acceptable to moderates – and a public that is increasingly angry about the Iran war and the influence of Tel Aviv over Washington.

The latest Democratic primaries in Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota have shown that, while hardcore DSA messaging still meets fierce resistance among even Democratic voters, a kind of DSA-lite politics – which signals its socialist virtue without ever being too explicit – can win.

And although often teased for pretending to have grown up poorer than she did, AOC does at least have a plausible working-class backstory as a Puerto Rican waitress from the Bronx. She can be a radical for normies, in other words. And, after the brash billionaire Trump, that might be all it takes to reach the White House.

news.title: With increasing enthusiasm, Democrats are embracing need for Supreme Court reforms
news.text:
A few months ago, Kevin Kruse, a historian at Princeton University, explained that Franklin Roosevelt’s court-packing plan in 1937 failed to gain traction for a foundational reason: The Supreme Court was still widely perceived at the time as apolitical, making presidential encroachment seem like an unwarranted abuse.

“This court, however, is nakedly partisan,” Kruse added. “And any Democrat in power should be saying so early and often.”

There’s ample public opinion research to suggest that attitudes toward the high court have, in fact, shifted significantly in recent years. The latest Pew Research Center poll, for example, released two weeks ago, showed favorable views of the institution hovering at generational lows. The same week, the latest Gallup poll showed public confidence in the Supreme Court falling to a record low of just 33%.

As for Kruse’s advice to Democratic officials, many of the party’s leaders and prominent voices appear to be thinking along similar lines. NBC News reported:

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said today that he is in favor of “dramatic” Supreme Court reform and intends to push for it should Democrats flip the House come November.

“The Supreme Court, the conservative right-wing majority on the Supreme Court, has become basically a subsidiary of the MAGA Republican Party,” Jeffries said in an interview at the National Association of Black Journalists’ convention in Atlanta.

The Democratic leader, who will be positioned to be elected speaker if the party takes back the House majority, said the justices seem to believe “the status quo is acceptable. It’s not.”

Jeffries didn’t elaborate on the specific reforms he had in mind, though the New York Democrat said there are “a variety of different options that are on the table,” and he’s not prepared to “foreclose any single one of them.”

If it seems leading Democratic voices are embracing similar stances with increasing frequency and enthusiasm, it’s not your imagination. Just two weeks ago, former Vice President Kamala Harris spoke at the National Urban League’s annual conference and said, “We need to revisit the point of expanding the court to 13 justices like we have 13 district courts.”

A month earlier, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro voiced support for “radical reform” to the Supreme Court, which came on the heels of Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia agreeing that “all options have to be on the table” when it comes to changing the high court.

This week, Sen. Adam Schiff of California wrote an opinion piece for The Los Angeles Times, making the case for “urgent” reform.

“It’s no secret that the Supreme Court has become an extension of our partisan politics over the past decade,” Schiff said in his op-ed. “The decisions handed down in the 2026 session prove just how broken the court has become and how unrepresentative it is of the views of the American people.”

In the coming months, there will likely be plenty of debate among advocates about the kind of changes to pursue and the political viability of the competing ideas. It’s also a safe bet that many reformers will disagree with one another about the details. But the bottom line remains the same: In Democratic politics, the conversation has shifted rapidly to how, not whether, to reform the Supreme Court.

As many in the party start eyeing the 2028 presidential race, don’t be surprised if this becomes a litmus-test issue for many Democratic voters.
